Spherical Fixed-Point Reasoners:
Adaptive Loop Halting on the Hypersphere

Arber Zela Affiliation: EPFL    Artavazd Maranjyan Affiliation: EPFL    Pol Puigdemont Affiliation: EPFL    David Berghaus Affiliation: Lamarr Institute Affiliation: Fraunhofer IAIS    Valentyn Boreiko   Volkan Cevher Affiliation: EPFL Affiliation: Amazon AGI
Abstract

Looped (weight-tied) transformers enable adaptive computation by allocating more iterations to harder inputs. Fixed-Point Reasoners (FPRM) achieve this with a damped fixed-point solver, but operate in an unbounded Euclidean residual space with coupled rescaling and relative-norm halting. We introduce Spherical Fixed-Point Reasoners (SFPRM), which performs the same computation on the unit hypersphere of normalized transformers (nGPT). Input injection, damping, and halting become geodesic operations, yielding boundedness by construction and eliminating coefficient coupling. We prove fixed-point existence, local convergence under an explicit step-size condition, and global convergence under strong injection. On Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard and Mini-ARC, SFPRM achieves 96.6%96.6\%, 87.9%87.9\% and 59.1%59.1\% test accuracy, respectively, outperforming FPRM and other baselines while allocating test-time compute more effectively. Its converged geometry is also interpretable: token–input angles capture puzzle structure and predict correctness.

1 Introduction

Scaling test-time computation has become the main lever for improving the reasoning ability of sequence models, most visibly through chain-of-thought traces (Wei et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Cobbe et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2023; Snell et al., 2025). Looped transformers offer a latent alternative (Dehghani et al., 2019; Bai et al., 2019; Geiping et al., 2025): a single weight-tied block is applied repeatedly, so depth becomes an iteration count chosen at inference time, and compute can be allocated per input according to its difficulty. On algorithmic puzzles such as Sudoku, mazes, and ARC, this recipe lets small recursive reasoners compete with far larger models (Wang et al., 2025; Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025; Movahedi et al., 2026).

A looped transformer raises two questions: when should it stop, and will it stay well-behaved as it runs? The fixed-point view (Bai et al., 2019), answers the first by treating the loop as a solver for 𝐳⋆=Fθ​(𝐳⋆,𝐱)\mathbf{z}^{\star}=F_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}^{\star};\mathbf{x}) and halting once the iterate stops moving. Fixed-Point Reasoners (FPRM) (Movahedi et al., 2026) turn this into a practical recipe: a damped iteration whose step size decays on a patience rule, a relative-norm residual as the halting test, and a boundedness theorem that keeps the recurrent state from diverging. The second question is where the Euclidean formulation shows its cost. Because the residual stream is free to grow, a boundedness theorem must couple four residual-rescaling coefficients, and the halting residual needs a normalization factor to be scale-invariant.

We introduce Spherical Fixed-Point Reasoning Models (SFPRM), which run FPRM’s damped solver on nGPT’s (Loshchilov et al., 2025) unit sphere (Figure 1). The normalized Transformer (nGPT) obtains stable dynamics by changing the geometry rather than adding control: every hidden state lives on the unit hypersphere 𝕊d−1\mathbb{S}^{d-1} and each sub-layer is a learned angular move followed by renormalization, so the divergence FPRM must guard against cannot occur. Every control quantity of the loop becomes an angle: the input is re-injected by moving a fraction λ\lambda of the great-circle arc toward it, the damped update is a spherical linear interpolation (Slerp\Slerp) whose coefficient ηi\eta_{i} is an angular step size that FPRM’s patience-based decay literally shrinks, and the halting residual is the worst-token angle between an iterate and its proposal. Our contributions are:

  1. (i)

    Simplicity: because the state cannot leave the sphere, boundedness is structural, and FPRM’s coupled residual-rescaling coefficients, its boundedness theorem, and its relative-norm residual disappear rather than being re-proved;

  2. (ii)

    guarantees: a fixed point exists from continuity and input injection alone, with no contraction or Lipschitz assumption; angular damping stabilizes any fixed point whose tangent Jacobian has real parts below one, with an explicit step-size window; and sufficiently strong injection makes it a unique global attractor;

  3. (iii)

    performance: on Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Hard, SFPRM halts up to 2.7×2.7\times earlier than FPRM at equal or higher accuracy; and

  4. (iv)

    interpretability: the angle between each token state and its input anchor separates token classes during the recursion, converges to a readable encoding of the task’s structure, and, on Sudoku, predicts whether the answer is correct.

2 Related Work

Looped and weight-tied transformers. Tying the weights of a transformer block (Vaswani et al., 2017) and applying it repeatedly turns depth into an iteration count at inference time (Dehghani et al., 2019; Lan et al., 2020). Looped models match much deeper non-looped ones on synthetic reasoning tasks and can simulate chain-of-thought in latent space (Saunshi et al., 2025), learn in-context algorithms more sample-efficiently (Yang et al., 2024; Gatmiry et al., 2024), emulate programmable computation (Giannou et al., 2023), generalize in length when the loop matches the algorithm’s recursion (Fan et al., 2025), scale to billions of parameters (Geiping et al., 2025; Prairie et al., 2026), and supply a scaling axis for masked diffusion models (Carballo-Castro et al., 2026; Miele et al., 2026). SFPRM is a looped transformer whose loop is run as a fixed-point solve on the sphere.

Equilibrium models, adaptive computation, and halting. Adaptive Computation Time (Graves, 2016) and PonderNet (Banino et al., 2021) learn a halting distribution through an auxiliary loss, so halting is a learned head rather than a property of the dynamics. Recent methods such as HRM (Wang et al., 2025), URM (Gao et al., 2025), TRM (Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025), and PTRM (Sghaier et al., 2026) inherit this design. Deep equilibrium models (Bai et al., 2019; Bai et al., 2020; Winston and Kolter, 2020; Bai et al., 2021) replace the unrolled iteration by the fixed point of a weight-tied layer and differentiate implicitly through it. Attractor models (Fein-Ashley and Rashidinejad, 2026) and equilibrium reasoners (Huang et al., 2026) make the loop’s attractor explicit and halt on a solver tolerance or a residual-based selection, and FPRM (Movahedi et al., 2026) halts on a scale-invariant residual of the tied block itself, at the cost of coupled residual-rescaling coefficients that keep its Euclidean residual stream bounded; iterating past the point where the answer has settled is itself harmful (Bansal et al., 2022; Schwarzschild et al., 2021). Table 1 sorts these reasoners by whether a numerical fixed-point solve is performed and what governs halting; SFPRM alone combines a genuine solve with an intrinsic, scale-free halting criterion on a curved state space.

Normalized and hyperspherical representations. Constraining representations to a sphere is a long-standing stabilization device, for parameters (Salimans and Kingma, 2016; Miyato et al., 2018), latent variables (Davidson et al., 2018), contrastive representations (Wang and Isola, 2020), and flow language models that rotate tokens on 𝕊d−1\mathbb{S}^{d-1} (Deschenaux and Gülçehre, 2026). nGPT (Loshchilov et al., 2025) carries the constraint through an entire transformer, with every hidden state and weight vector on 𝕊d−1\mathbb{S}^{d-1} and each sub-layer a normalized retraction toward a learned target. SFPRM adopts that block, hence every optimizer and solver step becomes an angular update.

3 Spherical Fixed-Point Reasoning Models

3.1 Preliminaries

Notation. For a sequence of TT tokens with hidden dimension dd, the recurrent state at loop iteration ii is 𝐳i=(zi,1,…,zi,T)\mathbf{z}_{i}=(z_{i,1},\ldots,z_{i,T}) with token states zi,t∈ℝdz_{i,t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. We use ii for loop iterations, tt for token positions, and ℓ\ell for sub-layers. 𝕊d−1:={z∈ℝd:∥z∥=1}\mathbb{S}^{d-1}:=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\lVert z\rVert=1\} denotes the unit hypersphere in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. The embedded input is 𝐱=(x1,…,xT)\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T}). Tuples carry the product inner product ⟨𝐮,𝐯⟩:=∑t=1T⟨ut,vt⟩\langle\mathbf{u},\,\mathbf{v}\rangle:=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\langle u_{t},\,v_{t}\rangle and norm ∥𝐮∥2:=∑t=1T∥ut∥22\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert^{2}:=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\lVert u_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}. Lowercase fθf_{\theta} always denotes the weight-tied network, uppercase Fθ​(⋅,𝐱)F_{\theta}(\cdot\,;\mathbf{x}) the complete input-dependent recurrent map, and hϕh_{\phi} the readout.

Looped transformers and fixed-point reasoning. A looped Transformer applies a weight-tied network repeatedly to a state that is re-exposed to the same input 𝐱\mathbf{x} at every application: 𝐳i+1=Fθ​(𝐳i,𝐱)\mathbf{z}_{i+1}=F_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{i};\mathbf{x}), for i=0,1,…i=0,1,\ldots, and predicts with a readout hϕ​(𝐳i)h_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}_{i}). A convergent iteration reaches a fixed point 𝐳⋆=Fθ​(𝐳⋆,𝐱)\mathbf{z}^{\star}=F_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}^{\star};\mathbf{x}), the equilibrium view of Bai et al. (2019). The prediction is determined by the fixed point, while the number of iterations needed to reach it is chosen per input. FPRM (Movahedi et al., 2026) uses a pre-norm block of depth DD (2​D2D attention and MLP sub-layers). Because the residual stream is free to grow indefinitely, FPRM uses tied residual coefficients (α1,β1)(\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}) and iteration-level coefficients (α2,β2)(\alpha_{2},\beta_{2}):

𝐳iℓ=α1𝐳iℓ−1+β1fθℓℓ(Normpre(𝐳iℓ−1)),ℓ=1,…,2D,𝐳i+10=α2𝐳i2​D+β2𝐱.\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\ell}=\alpha_{1}\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\ell-1}+\beta_{1}f_{\theta^{\ell}}^{\ell}\!\left(\Norm_{\mathrm{pre}}(\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\ell-1})\right),\quad\ell=1,\ldots,2D,\qquad\mathbf{z}_{i+1}^{0}=\alpha_{2}\mathbf{z}_{i}^{2D}+\beta_{2}\mathbf{x}. (1)

Via a boundedness theorem that couples the four coefficients:,

β2=1−α2​α12​D,β1=β2​(1−α1)1−α12​D,0≤α1,α2<1,\textstyle\beta_{2}=1-\alpha_{2}\alpha_{1}^{2D},\qquad\beta_{1}=\frac{\beta_{2}(1-\alpha_{1})}{1-\alpha_{1}^{2D}},\qquad 0\leq\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}<1, (2)

ensures that the recurrent carry path (gain α2​α12​D\alpha_{2}\alpha_{1}^{2D}) is balanced against the injected input. Given a proposal 𝐳~i=Fθ​(𝐳i,𝐱)\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}=F_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{i};\mathbf{x}), FPRM damps linearly:

𝐳i+1=(1−ηi)​𝐳i+ηi​𝐳~i,\mathbf{z}_{i+1}=(1-\eta_{i})\mathbf{z}_{i}+\eta_{i}\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}, (3)

with a per-sample ηi∈(0,1]\eta_{i}\in(0,1] that is decayed on a patience rule whenever the residual stalls, and halts on the relative residual:

rE,i=∥𝐳i−𝐳~i∥∞∥𝐳~i∥∞+ϵ,∥𝐮∥∞:=max1≤t≤T, 1≤j≤d⁡|(ut)j|,\textstyle r_{\mathrm{E},i}=\frac{\lVert\mathbf{z}_{i}-\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}\rVert_{\infty}}{\lVert\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}\rVert_{\infty}+\epsilon},\qquad\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert_{\infty}:=\max_{1\leq t\leq T,\,1\leq j\leq d}|(u_{t})_{j}|, (4)

The coefficient coupling and the denominator of the residual exist to contain a Euclidean residual stream whose scale is not fixed. Rather than differentiate implicitly through the equilibrium as in Bai et al. (2019), FPRM trains with truncated BPTT over windows of KK iterations, deep supervision, and state detachment between windows.

nGPT and spherical geometry. nGPT (Loshchilov et al., 2025) constrains every hidden state to the unit sphere 𝕊d−1\mathbb{S}^{d-1} via Norm⁡(u)=u/∥u∥2\Norm(u)=u/\lVert u\rVert_{2} for a nonzero token vector and folds each sub-layer output into the state through learned, per-coordinate eigen learning rates αA,αM∈ℝd\alpha_{A},\alpha_{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:

𝐳\displaystyle\mathbf{z} ←Norm⁡(𝐳+αA⊙(Norm⁡(Attn⁡(𝐳))−𝐳)),\displaystyle\leftarrow\Norm\!\big(\mathbf{z}+\alpha_{A}\odot(\Norm(\Attn(\mathbf{z}))-\mathbf{z})\big), (5)
𝐳\displaystyle\mathbf{z} ←Norm⁡(𝐳+αM⊙(Norm⁡(MLP⁡(𝐳))−𝐳)).\displaystyle\leftarrow\Norm\!\big(\mathbf{z}+\alpha_{M}\odot(\Norm(\MLP(\mathbf{z}))-\mathbf{z})\big).

Norm\Norm acts token-wise on tuples, and αA,αM\alpha_{A},\alpha_{M} are shared across tokens. Each sub-layer is a normalized retraction toward a learned target, so unit norm is preserved by construction rather than enforced by a constraint (Absil et al., 2008). For unit vectors u,vu,v write ∠⁡(u,v):=arccos⁡(⟨u,v⟩)\angle(u,v):=\arccosop(\langle u,\,v\rangle). For Ω=∠⁡(u,v)∈(0,π)\Omega=\angle(u,v)\in(0,\pi), the spherical linear interpolation:

Slerpη⁡(u,v)=sin⁡((1−η)​Ω)sin⁡Ω​u+sin⁡(η​Ω)sin⁡Ω​v,η∈[0,1],\textstyle\Slerp_{\eta}(u,v)=\frac{\sin((1-\eta)\Omega)}{\sin\Omega}\,u+\frac{\sin(\eta\Omega)}{\sin\Omega}\,v,\qquad\eta\in[0,1], (6)

moves a fraction η\eta along the shortest great-circle arc from uu to vv and stays on the sphere. For coincident endpoints we set Slerpη⁡(u,u):=u\Slerp_{\eta}(u,u):=u, the limit of eq. 6 as v→uv\to u; at an antipodal pair (v=−uv=-u) the shortest arc is not unique, so we use eq. 12 (Section A.2). For small Ω\Omega, Slerp\Slerp agrees with normalized linear interpolation Norm⁡((1−η)​u+η​v)\Norm((1-\eta)u+\eta v) up to O⁡(Ω3)O(\Omega^{3}) (Lemma 2).

3.2 SFPRM: the recurrent map and its solver

SFPRM is a looped Transformer model whose recurrent state lives on the unit hypersphere and whose loop is run as a damped fixed-point solver. Algorithm 1 places it next to FPRM (Movahedi et al., 2026), its Euclidean predecessor. Every difference is a Euclidean operation replaced by its spherical one: the state is confined to 𝒮\mathcal{S} by a weight-tied nGPT block (line 6, eq. 5), affine injection becomes a geodesic move a fraction λ\lambda of the arc toward the input (line 5, eq. 8), the relative residual becomes the chordal one (line 7, eq. 9), and linear damping becomes a rotation a fraction ηi\eta_{i} of the way toward the proposal (line 10, eq. 10).

State space and spherical block. SFPRM’s recurrent state is a tuple of unit token vectors, 𝐳i=(zi,1,…,zi,T)∈𝒮:=(𝕊d−1)T\mathbf{z}_{i}=(z_{i,1},\ldots,z_{i,T})\in\mathcal{S}:=(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})^{T}, where ∥zi,t∥2=1\lVert z_{i,t}\rVert_{2}=1 and the input 𝐱=(x1,…,xT)∈𝒮\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T})\in\mathcal{S} is the embedded sequence normalized token-wise. The weight-tied network fθ:𝒮→𝒮f_{\theta}:\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{S} is a stack of DD nGPT layers, each an attention retraction followed by an MLP retraction as in eq. 5, with QK-normalization and eigen learning rates shared across iterations. Attention couples tokens, so fθf_{\theta} acts on the product 𝒮\mathcal{S} rather than token by token; it is the block applied at every iteration in eq. 8. Following nGPT’s logit scaling, predictions are read out as sz​hϕ​(𝐳)s_{z}\,h_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}), where, given the vocabulary 𝒱\mathcal{V}, hϕh_{\phi} is a linear map ℝd→ℝ|𝒱|\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|} and szs_{z} is a learned scalar. nGPT would normalize the rows of ϕ\phi like every other weight vector, however we keep them unnormalized so the head can set its own per-class scale while the state stays on the sphere.

Geodesic input injection. We lift Slerp\Slerp from tokens to sequences by applying it position-wise. Given two unit token vectors 𝐮\mathbf{u} and 𝐯\mathbf{v}, we write:

Slerpη⁡(𝐮,𝐯):=(Slerpη⁡(ut,vt))t=1T,η∈[0,1].\textstyle\Slerp_{\eta}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}):=\bigl(\Slerp_{\eta}(u_{t},v_{t})\bigr)_{t=1}^{T},\qquad\eta\in[0,1]. (7)

At every iteration ii, the current state is first pulled toward the input along the shortest arc using Slerpλ\Slerp_{\lambda} of eq. 7, and the result is then passed through the nGPT block of eq. 5:

Fθ​(𝐳,𝐱):=fθ​(Slerpλ⁡(𝐳,𝐱)),0<λ<1.F_{\theta}(\mathbf{z};\mathbf{x}):=f_{\theta}\!\left(\Slerp_{\lambda}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{x})\right),\qquad 0<\lambda<1. (8)

The injection strength λ\lambda is a model parameter, fixed or learned, with the same reading in either case: it is the fraction of the arc from each token state to its input token that is traversed before the block is applied. Geodesic injection is the intrinsic form of FPRM’s additive mixing α2​𝐳+β2​𝐱\alpha_{2}\mathbf{z}+\beta_{2}\mathbf{x} (eq. 1): normalizing any positive combination α​u+β​v\alpha u+\beta v lands on the same shortest arc from u^\widehat{u} to v^\widehat{v}, at a fraction set by the coefficients, the norms, and the angle (Lemma 3 in Section A.3). FPRM’s coefficients therefore do two jobs at once: they place the state along this arc, and, through the coupling (eq. 2), they keep its norm from drifting. On the unit sphere the second part is given by construction, and the first is done by λ\lambda alone. SFPRM thus replaces the implicit, state-dependent fraction by a single parameter and drops (α1,β1,α2,β2)(\alpha_{1},\beta_{1},\alpha_{2},\beta_{2}) together with their coupling.

Scale-free halting residual. Given the same proposal 𝐳~i=Fθ​(𝐳i,𝐱)\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}=F_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{i};\mathbf{x}) of eq. 8, geodesic distance on 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the angle between unit vectors, so SFPRM halts on the worst-token chordal residual, which is smooth where the angle itself is not:

rc,i=max1≤t≤T⁡ρi,t,ρi,t:=1−⟨zi,t,z~i,t⟩=12​∥zi,t−z~i,t∥22,\textstyle r_{\mathrm{c},i}=\max_{1\leq t\leq T}\rho_{i,t},\qquad\rho_{i,t}:=1-\langle z_{i,t},\,\widetilde{z}_{i,t}\rangle=\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert z_{i,t}-\widetilde{z}_{i,t}\rVert_{2}^{2}, (9)

and halts once rc,i<τcr_{\mathrm{c},i}<\tau_{c}, where τc=1−cos⁡τang\tau_{c}=1-\cos\tau_{\mathrm{ang}} for an angular tolerance τang\tau_{\mathrm{ang}}, so the test fires exactly when every token’s proposal lies within τang\tau_{\mathrm{ang}} of its iterate. The worst token maxt\max_{t} is the spherical analogue of the maximum over tokens and coordinates in rE,ir_{\mathrm{E},i} (eq. 4): a few unconverged but decisive tokens should keep the iteration running. What FPRM’s denominator and ϵ\epsilon provide is scale invariance, and on the unit sphere that is automatic, so neither is needed. The two tests remain inequivalent: ρi,t\rho_{i,t} sees only the geodesic angle and so accepts a disk of radius τang\tau_{\mathrm{ang}} around the iterate, whereas rE,ir_{\mathrm{E},i} sees the largest-magnitude coordinate and so accepts an axis-aligned ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} region whose angular extent depends on the direction of the update, and two proposals at the same angle can get opposite verdicts (Figure 2). We adopt the chordal form for its simplicity and frame-independence.

Geodesic damping. If the residual is above tolerance, the state is advanced by a rotation toward the proposal, in place of FPRM’s linear interpolation (eq. 3):

𝐳i+1:=Slerpηi⁡(𝐳i,𝐳~i),0<ηi≤1.\mathbf{z}_{i+1}:=\Slerp_{\eta_{i}}(\mathbf{z}_{i},\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}),\qquad 0<\eta_{i}\leq 1. (10)

By Lemma 1, token tt turns by exactly ηi​∠​(zi,t,z~i,t)\eta_{i}\,\angle(z_{i,t},\widetilde{z}_{i,t}), so ηi\eta_{i} is an angular step size: ηi=1\eta_{i}=1 applies the raw map and smaller values shrink the rotation without leaving the sphere, so the block is always evaluated on the geometry it was trained on. The update never changes the equilibria: for ηi>0\eta_{i}>0 the step returns 𝐳i\mathbf{z}_{i} if and only if 𝐳~i=𝐳i\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}=\mathbf{z}_{i}, so the damped iteration and FθF_{\theta} have exactly the same fixed points wherever the arcs are defined. As in FPRM (eq. 3), ηi\eta_{i} is per sample, starts at 11, and is multiplied by γ<1\gamma<1 whenever the residual has not improved for PP iterations. On the sphere this patience rule is literally a shrinking of the per-iteration rotation angle, a derivative-free search for a step inside the stability window of Theorem 1.

Training. Training follows FPRM: deep supervision with truncated BPTT, i.e., each optimizer step backpropagating through one segment of KK geodesic steps with the state detached between segments. The residual, patience counter and step-size schedule are computed from detached states, so they steer the solver without entering the gradient; differentiating Norm\Norm projects state cotangents onto the tangent space, parameters stay Euclidean, and weight vectors are renormalized after every optimizer step. In practice, we use a guarded Slerp\Slerp (eq. 12), which replaces the sine formula by normalized linear interpolation near coincident endpoints and by an explicit arc near antipodes.

3.2.1 Theoretical guarantees

We now investigate what the geometry buys analytically. All statements concern the exact recurrence eqs. 8 to 10 with shortest-arc interpolation. Full proofs are in Appendix A.

Boundedness by construction. Because injection and damping return unit token vectors (Lemma 1), the block does so by construction (eq. 5), and so does every branch of the guarded step (Lemma 2), the state stays on 𝒮\mathcal{S} for every ii and every θ\theta: recurrent magnitudes can neither explode nor vanish, which is what FPRM’s boundedness theorem secures through the coefficient constraints in eq. 2. However, boundedness alone says nothing about whether a fixed point exists or is reached, which is what we address next.

Input injection guarantees a fixed point. On a sphere, continuity alone does not guarantee a fixed point since rotating a circle moves every point. Input injection repairs this by moving each token a fraction λ\lambda of the way to its input, keeping every injected state in the cap 𝒞𝐱:={𝐲∈𝒮:∠⁡(yt,xt)≤(1−λ)​π​ for every token ​t}\mathcal{C}_{\mathbf{x}}:=\left\{\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{S}:\ \angle(y_{t},x_{t})\leq(1-\lambda)\pi\text{ for every token }t\right\}, which, unlike the sphere, can be flattened into a closed ball, where every continuous self-map has a fixed point.

Proposition 1 (Fixed-point existence).

Fix 𝐱\mathbf{x} and 0<λ<10<\lambda<1. Assume fθf_{\theta} is continuous on 𝒞𝐱\mathcal{C}_{\mathbf{x}} and fθ​(𝐲)t≠−xt​ for every ​𝐲∈𝒞𝐱​ and token ​tf_{\theta}(\mathbf{y})_{t}\neq-x_{t}\text{ for every }\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathbf{x}}\text{ and token }t. Then the recurrent map Fθ​(⋅,𝐱)F_{\theta}(\cdot\,;\mathbf{x}) in eq. 8 has at least one fixed point 𝐳⋆=Fθ​(𝐳⋆,𝐱)\mathbf{z}^{\star}=F_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}^{\star};\mathbf{x}) in 𝒮\mathcal{S}.

The full proof (Appendix A.4) applies Brouwer’s theorem (Brouwer, 1911; Ortega and Rheinboldt, 1970) to the reversed composition H⁡(𝐲):=Slerpλ⁡(fθ​(𝐲),𝐱)H(\mathbf{y}):=\Slerp_{\lambda}(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}),\mathbf{x}). Unlike FθF_{\theta}, which injects before the block, HH ends with the injection, so it maps the cap into itself, and the antipode assumption keeps it well defined and continuous; its fixed point 𝐲⋆\mathbf{y}^{\star} gives the fixed point 𝐳⋆:=fθ​(𝐲⋆)\mathbf{z}^{\star}:=f_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}^{\star}) of FθF_{\theta}. No Lipschitz constant, contraction modulus, or spectral bound on fθf_{\theta} is needed. FPRM proves existence only via global convergence, hence under contraction (Movahedi et al., 2026, Theorem 2); Brouwer alone would need the coefficient coupling that keeps a ball invariant. On the sphere compactness is structural and injection supplies the missing ball-shaped domain. Only 𝐲⋆\mathbf{y}^{\star}, however, provably lies in 𝒞𝐱\mathcal{C}_{\mathbf{x}}, and existence implies neither uniqueness nor attraction, which the next two results address.

Angular damping stabilizes a fixed point. Let 𝐳⋆\mathbf{z}^{\star} be a fixed point of Fθ​(⋅,𝐱)F_{\theta}(\cdot\,;\mathbf{x}) and let J:=D𝐳​Fθ​(𝐳⋆,𝐱)J:=D_{\mathbf{z}}F_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}^{\star};\mathbf{x}) be its Jacobian in the recurrent state at 𝐳⋆\mathbf{z}^{\star}, with θ\theta and 𝐱\mathbf{x} held fixed. Since FθF_{\theta} maps 𝒮\mathcal{S} to itself, JJ sends tangent perturbations 𝐮=(ut)t=1T\mathbf{u}=(u_{t})_{t=1}^{T} with ⟨ut,zt⋆⟩=0\langle u_{t},\,z_{t}^{\star}\rangle=0 to tangent perturbations, and we regard it as an endomorphism of that T⁡(d−1)T(d-1)-dimensional tangent space. It contains all coupling between tokens through attention and need be neither orthogonal nor diagonalizable.

Theorem 1 (Local convergence of angular damping).

Suppose Fθ​(⋅,𝐱)F_{\theta}(\cdot\,;\mathbf{x}) is differentiable at a fixed point 𝐳⋆\mathbf{z}^{\star} and every ζ∈σ⁡(J)\zeta\in\sigma(J), where σ⁡(J)\sigma(J) is the Jacobian’s set of eigenvalues, satisfies Re⁡(ζ)<1\Real(\zeta)<1. Then for every fixed 0<η≤10<\eta\leq 1 with

η<ηmax:=minζ∈σ⁡(J)⁡2​(1−Re⁡(ζ))|ζ−1|2,\textstyle\eta<\eta_{\max}:=\min_{\zeta\in\sigma(J)}\frac{2\bigl(1-\Real(\zeta)\bigr)}{|\zeta-1|^{2}}, (11)

the damped iteration 𝐳i+1=Slerpη⁡(𝐳i,Fθ​(𝐳i,𝐱))\mathbf{z}_{i+1}=\Slerp_{\eta}\!\left(\mathbf{z}_{i},F_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{i};\mathbf{x})\right) converges to 𝐳⋆\mathbf{z}^{\star} from every sufficiently close initial state, with ∥𝐳i−𝐳⋆∥≤C​qi​∥𝐳0−𝐳⋆∥\lVert\mathbf{z}_{i}-\mathbf{z}^{\star}\rVert\leq Cq^{i}\lVert\mathbf{z}_{0}-\mathbf{z}^{\star}\rVert for some C>0C>0 and q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1). Moreover, wherever the shortest arcs are defined, the damped iteration and FθF_{\theta} have exactly the same fixed points.

This is the spherical counterpart of FPRM’s stabilization result (Movahedi et al., 2026, Theorem 3), with an explicit window and with unit norm and fixed points preserved. The window is certified for a fixed η\eta; the patience rule (lines 8–9 of Algorithm 1) searches for one heuristically, without guarantee. The proof (Appendix A.6) linearizes the damped step at 𝐳⋆\mathbf{z}^{\star} to (1−η)​Id+η​J(1-\eta)\operatorname{Id}+\eta J (Lemma 4), which moves each eigenvalue ζ\zeta of JJ a fraction η\eta from 11 toward ζ\zeta; the window of eq. 11 is exactly what keeps them all inside the unit disk. A spectral radius below one then gives geometric convergence in tangent coordinates, which the coordinate map transfers to the state. Such an η\eta exists only if Re⁡(ζ)<1\Real(\zeta)<1 for every ζ\zeta: damping tames modes that oscillate or spiral away under the raw map, not expansive ones with Re⁡(ζ)≥1\Real(\zeta)\geq 1, which training must remove (Remark 1).

Global convergence under strong injection. Finally, we identify a regime where the raw recurrence (η=1\eta=1) converges from every admissible initialization. 𝐱\mathbf{x} and fθf_{\theta} are held fixed while λ\lambda varies.

Theorem 2 (Global convergence under strong input injection).

Suppose fθ:𝒮→𝒮f_{\theta}:\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{S} is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of 𝐱\mathbf{x} and fθ​(𝐱)t≠−xtf_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})_{t}\neq-x_{t} for every token tt. Then there exists a λ0∈(0,1)\lambda_{0}\in(0,1), depending on fθf_{\theta} and 𝐱\mathbf{x}, such that for every λ∈(λ0,1)\lambda\in(\lambda_{0},1) the map Fθ​(⋅,𝐱)F_{\theta}(\cdot\,;\mathbf{x}) has a fixed point 𝐳⋆\mathbf{z}^{\star}, unique among all states at which the input interpolation is defined. For each such λ\lambda and every 𝐳0∈𝒮\mathbf{z}_{0}\in\mathcal{S} with z0,t≠−xtz_{0,t}\neq-x_{t} for all tt, the iterates 𝐳i+1=Fθ​(𝐳i,𝐱)\mathbf{z}_{i+1}=F_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{i};\mathbf{x}) are well defined and satisfy ∥𝐳i−𝐳⋆∥≤C​qi−1\lVert\mathbf{z}_{i}-\mathbf{z}^{\star}\rVert\leq Cq^{i-1} for all i≥1i\geq 1, with C>0C>0 and q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1) independent of 𝐳0\mathbf{z}_{0}.

The proof (Appendix A.7, with an explicit λ0\lambda_{0}) uses logarithmic coordinates at 𝐱\mathbf{x}, where injection multiplies by 1−λ1-\lambda: for λ\lambda near one, the first injection pulls every admissible state into a small ball around 𝐱\mathbf{x} on which the map is a Banach contraction, so only that ball matters. FPRM’s global result (Movahedi et al., 2026, Theorem 2) instead rests on a global Lipschitz bound and a small residual coefficient, which the sphere lacks: injection does not contract near the input’s antipode. Together the three results cover every injection strength: a fixed point exists for all λ\lambda, strong injection makes it a unique global attractor, and damping gives local convergence under weaker injection.

4 Empirical Evaluation

With the following experiments we answer three research questions:

  1. (RQ1)

    Accuracy. How does SFPRM compare to FPRM and other recurrent reasoner baselines? Does constraining the recurrence on the sphere cost accuracy? (Section 4.1)

  2. (RQ2)

    Convergence and halting. How effectively does SFPRM utilize the learned recurrence under the angular halting criterion and is the fixed-point unique? (Section 4.2)

  3. (RQ3)

    Geometry of the computation. What does the fixed-point iteration write into the state, and does the spherical parameterization make it readable? (Section 4.3)

Setup. We evaluate SFPRM on puzzle benchmarks: Maze-Hard, Sudoku-Extreme (Wang et al., 2025), Mini-ARC (Kim et al., 2022) and ARC-1 (Chollet et al., 2024), used to assess generalization when trained with a limited number of examples. SFPRM and FPRM share a 6.836.83M-parameter Transformer backbone and follow the hyperparameters of Movahedi et al. (2026) (details in Appendix B). SFPRM trains its weight matrices with Muon (Jordan et al., 2024) and its embeddings, normalization scales, and scalars with AdamW, regularizes with variational and weight dropout, and learns the injection fraction λ\lambda, except on Sudoku (λ\lambda fixed at 0.10.1). It halts once rc,i<τc=0.01r_{\mathrm{c},i}<\tau_{c}=0.01 (eq. 9), i.e. once every token’s proposal lies within 8.1∘8.1^{\circ} of its iterate.

4.1 RQ1: accuracy on puzzle benchmarks

Table 2 compares SFPRM with published recurrent reasoners. On Sudoku-Extreme, SFPRM reaches 96.6%96.6\% exact accuracy, 2.42.4 points above FPRM published results. Since we cannot resample the same 11k base puzzles augmented 1000×1000\times from FPRM, we train it on 55k puzzles augmented 200×200\times instead: the same number of training examples, but five times as many distinct puzzles. On Maze-Hard, SFPRM reaches 87.9%87.9\% on the 1,0001{,}000 test mazes, above TRM’s and FPRM’s published results and behind only the 2727M-parameter Attractor model (Fein-Ashley and Rashidinejad, 2026). On Mini-ARC, SFPRM reaches 59.1%59.1\% Pass@1, above both the best published result in its size group (EqR, 55.3%55.3\% (Huang et al., 2026)) and all baselines retrained under our protocol (FPRM 55.0%55.0\%, HRM 51.7%51.7\%, EqR 40.3%40.3\%, TRM 36.9%36.9\%). On ARC-1, it matches FPRM.

Answer to RQ1. Confining the state to the sphere improves accuracy: SFPRM outperforms FPRM and other baselines on Sudoku-Extreme (96.6%96.6\% vs. 94.2%94.2\%), Maze-Hard (87.9%87.9\% vs. 87.0%87.0\%) and Mini-ARC (59.1%59.1\% vs. 55.0%55.0\%), and matches it on ARC-1 (47.4%47.4\% vs. 47.5%47.5\%).

4.2 RQ2: convergence and halting

Loop utilization and halting. To see how the two solvers converge and when they stop, we run each trained model with halting disabled for NmaxN_{\max} iterations, decode every iterate 𝐳i\mathbf{z}_{i}, and record the residual its solver tests. Halting is counted per sequence, i.e., a sequence halts once its residual stays below the threshold (Appendix C.4). Figure 3 shows the result on Maze and Figure 10 on Sudoku. Both residuals fall quickly, and both models saturate their accuracy within 2020–3535 iterations, so every later loop is spent after the answer stops changing. SFPRM converges faster and stops sooner: it halts on 992/1000992/1000 mazes against FPRM’s 950950, and on average 2222 iterations earlier (108108 vs. 130130).

Fixed-point uniqueness. Theorem 2 predicts that for λ>λ0\lambda>\lambda_{0} the raw recurrence 𝐳i+1=Fθ​(𝐳i,𝐱)\mathbf{z}_{i+1}=F_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{i};\mathbf{x}) contracts to one fixed point from every initialization. We test this by overriding λ\lambda at inference in the trained model (learned λ=0.47\lambda=0.47) and running the raw map, without damping, in fp32 for 400400 steps on 3232 evenly spaced test puzzles, from eight initializations each: six random states, the input 𝐱\mathbf{x}, and its antipode −𝐱-\mathbf{x}, which the theorem excludes. The largest geodesic angle between the eight end states measures uniqueness without a reference point (Figure 4a). For λ≥0.8\lambda\geq 0.8 all eight end states coincide on every puzzle. At the trained λ=0.47\lambda=0.47 the raw map reaches an attracting fixed point on 91%91\% of the puzzles, and on the puzzle of Figure 4b all eight paths end inside the exact-match region. At λ=0.1\lambda=0.1 the raw iteration does not converge, while for λ≥0.7\lambda\geq 0.7 it converges within a few steps to a unique fixed point that no longer solves the puzzle.

Varying the fixed-point solver. At inference we replace the damped step of Algorithm 1 by two standard solvers, keeping the model and the halting rule: Anderson acceleration (Anderson, 1965; Walker and Ni, 2011) and limited-memory Broyden (Broyden, 1965), the solver of deep equilibrium models (Bai et al., 2019). Both cost one evaluation of FθF_{\theta} per iteration, like the damped step (details in Appendix C.5). For both models Anderson halts earlier than the default solver, on every Maze example, while staying within one point of its accuracy (Table 5 and Figure 5). Broyden halts about as early on Maze but diverges afterwards, so it relies on stopping in time. Without damping (η=1\eta=1), 3737–100%100\% of examples never reach τ\tau, and on Sudoku accuracy drops as well. We leave training with these solvers, rather than swapping them in at inference, for future work.

Answer to RQ2. SFPRM uses its loop iterations more effectively than FPRM: its angular criterion halts earlier on Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Hard at equal or higher accuracy. Under strong input injection the raw iteration converges to a unique fixed point, as Theorem 2 predicts.

4.3 RQ3: the geometry of the computation

The state reveals the task structure. On the sphere a token state’s only free quantity is its direction, so we probe the computation through the anchor angle ∠⁡(zi,t,xt)\angle(z_{i,t},x_{t}) between each cell’s iterate and its unit-normalized input embedding, the quantity that injection acts on (eq. 8).

Figure 7 shows four frames of one rollout per task (FPRM and more puzzles in Figures 21 and 22), and Figures 6 and 15 show the angle over loops for every cell of a test puzzle, clustered by cell class. On Sudoku, we can see that, for SFPRM, the clue tokens rotate toward their anchors while the blanks end near orthogonal. By i=39i{=}39 the anchor map is a binary image of the clue mask. Each loop iteration writes the cell class information into the direction of the state. On the other hand, FPRM encodes the mask mainly in the norm of its state (Figure 9), a scale set by training rather than by the geometry. Its anchor map shows only small differences between clues and blanks. Similarly, on Maze, SFPRM settles walls at ≈90∘{\approx}90^{\circ}, empty cells at ≈113∘{\approx}113^{\circ}, and path cells at ≈102∘{\approx}102^{\circ}. Empty and path cells receive the same input token but still end at different angles, so the looping itself decides which cells lie on the path instead of reading it off the input. FPRM separates walls from free cells but not path from empty cells. On Mini-ARC (Figures 8, 23 and 24), the cells a task rewrites end furthest from their anchors under SFPRM (mean AUC 0.810.81), while FPRM’s ordering varies across tasks (AUC 0.510.51).

The final angle predicts correctness. On unsolved Sudoku puzzles both SFPRM cell classes end farther from their anchors (Figure 9): the clues at ≈65∘{\approx}65^{\circ} instead of ≈52∘{\approx}52^{\circ}, almost disjoint from the solved ones, and the blanks at ≈92∘{\approx}92^{\circ} instead of ≈88∘{\approx}88^{\circ}. The converged angle thus flags a wrong answer without labels, shared by every cell and puzzle. FPRM’s final norms separate the two outcomes far less: its clue and blank norms overlap widely.

Answer to RQ3. SFPRM’s loop writes task structure into the state, and on the sphere it is legible as an angle to the input: the clue mask on Sudoku, the path on Maze, and, on Sudoku, whether the answer is correct. FPRM’s angles and state norm carry this structure only faintly or partially.

5 Conclusion

We introduced SFPRM, which runs FPRM’s damped fixed-point loop on nGPT’s hypersphere. This change of geometry assures norm boundedness by construction and eliminates the need for FPRM’s coupled residual-rescaling coefficients. We provide theoretical guarantees under weaker assumptions than its Euclidean counterpart. Empirically, on puzzle and reasoning tasks, SFPRM halts more effectively at equal or higher accuracy than FPRM. Finally, we showed that the angle each token keeps to its input turns out to be a readable encoding of the task’s structure and, on Sudoku, a label-free predictor of correctness. Natural next steps are to scale SFPRM to language modeling and train with better solvers, which we have so far used only at inference.

Reproducibility. We provide the experimental protocol in Appendix B and in Table 3 a list of the used hyperparameters in our experiments. The inference-time solver description and comparison from Section 4.2 is provided in Appendix C.5. We implemented SFPRM on top of the public FPRM code base (Movahedi et al., 2026). The code is provided at https://github.com/arberzela/sfprm.git. All runs were trained using Nvidia A100 GPUs for a single seed each.

LLM Usage. Running FPRM’s damped fixed-point solver on nGPT’s unit hypersphere, with geodesic injection, angular damping, and a chordal halting residual, was the authors’ idea. For the theory, the authors provided proof strategies and guidance, while AI tools helped develop, write, and check parts of the proofs. The SFPRM implementation on the FPRM code base was assisted by Claude and verified by the authors, who also produced the experimental design, analyses, and figures with LLM assistance. Claude helped restructure and edit the manuscript for length and readability.
