Appendix A Proofs for the SFPRM guarantees

Throughout this appendix, the already token-wise normalized input 𝐱∈𝒮\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{S} is fixed and

𝒮=(𝕊d−1)T,∠(u,v):=arccos(⟨u,v⟩),u,v∈𝕊d−1.\mathcal{S}=(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})^{T},\qquad\angle(u,v):=\arccosop(\langle u,\,v\rangle),\qquad u,v\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}.

The integer TT is the number of tokens. Every spherical operation is applied independently to the TT token vectors. In particular, we use the sequence-level convention from eq. 7. All operands passed to Norm\Norm are assumed nonzero. Exact Slerp\Slerp means interpolation along the unique shortest arc, so its endpoints are assumed non-antipodal. Numerical guards require separate care because an arbitrary antipodal fallback need not be continuous.

A.1 Basic geometry of spherical interpolation

Lemma 1 (Geometry of slerp).

Let u,v∈𝕊d−1u,v\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1} with v≠−uv\neq-u, and let s∈[0,1]s\in[0,1]. Then

∥Slerps⁡(u,v)∥2\displaystyle\lVert\Slerp_{s}(u,v)\rVert_{2} =1,\displaystyle=1,
∠⁡(u,Slerps⁡(u,v))\displaystyle\angle\!\left(u,\Slerp_{s}(u,v)\right) =s​∠​(u,v),\displaystyle=s\,\angle(u,v),
∠⁡(Slerps⁡(u,v),v)\displaystyle\angle\!\left(\Slerp_{s}(u,v),v\right) =(1−s)​∠​(u,v).\displaystyle=(1-s)\angle(u,v).

Moreover, if Ω:=∠⁡(u,v)>0\Omega:=\angle(u,v)>0, then

Slerps⁡(u,v)=cos⁡(s​Ω)​u+sin⁡(s​Ω)​e,e:=v−cos⁡Ω​usin⁡Ω,\Slerp_{s}(u,v)=\cos(s\Omega)\,u+\sin(s\Omega)\,e,\qquad e:=\frac{v-\cos\Omega\,u}{\sin\Omega},

where ee is a unit vector orthogonal to uu.

Proof.

Set Ω=∠⁡(u,v)\Omega=\angle(u,v). If Ω=0\Omega=0, then v=uv=u and Slerps⁡(u,u)=u\Slerp_{s}(u,u)=u by definition. Its norm is one and both angles are zero, proving all three claims in this case. For 0<Ω<π0<\Omega<\pi, define

e:=v−cos⁡Ω​usin⁡Ω.e:=\frac{v-\cos\Omega\,u}{\sin\Omega}.

Then ⟨u,e⟩=0\langle u,\,e\rangle=0, ∥e∥2=1\lVert e\rVert_{2}=1, and v=cos⁡Ω​u+sin⁡Ω​ev=\cos\Omega\,u+\sin\Omega\,e. Substituting this identity into the slerp formula and using the sine addition rule gives

Slerps⁡(u,v)=cos⁡(s​Ω)​u+sin⁡(s​Ω)​e.\Slerp_{s}(u,v)=\cos(s\Omega)u+\sin(s\Omega)e.

The two terms are orthogonal, so the result has unit norm. The same expression places it at angle s​Ωs\Omega from uu and (1−s)​Ω(1-s)\Omega from vv. ∎

A.2 Guarded interpolation

The implementation replaces exact slerp by a guarded step. The sine formula of eq. 6 gives 0/00/0 at Ω=0\Omega=0 and is ill conditioned nearby, especially in bf16, although Slerpη⁡(u,u)=u\Slerp_{\eta}(u,u)=u; at Ω=π\Omega=\pi the shortest arc is not unique. Write c=⟨u,v⟩c=\langle u,\,v\rangle and nlerpη⁡(u,v):=Norm⁡((1−η)​u+η​v)\nlerp_{\eta}(u,v):=\Norm\big((1-\eta)u+\eta v\big), and near an antipode fix an explicit arc through a unit vector e⁡(u,v)⟂ue(u,v)\perp u, namely e⁡(u,v)=Norm⁡(Pu​v)e(u,v)=\Norm(P_{u}v) with Pu=I−u​u⊤P_{u}=I-uu^{\top} when ∥Pu​v∥2>ϵv\lVert P_{u}v\rVert_{2}>\epsilon_{v} and a fixed unit vector e0​(u)⟂ue_{0}(u)\perp u otherwise. The guarded interpolation is

gSlerpη(u,v)={nlerpη⁡(u,v),c>1−ϵΩ,Arcη⁡(u,v):=cos⁡(η​Ω)​u+sin⁡(η​Ω)​e​(u,v),c<−1+ϵΩ,Slerpη⁡(u,v),otherwise.\gSlerp_{\eta}(u,v)=\begin{cases}\nlerp_{\eta}(u,v),&c>1-\epsilon_{\Omega},\\[2.0pt] \operatorname{Arc}_{\eta}(u,v):=\cos(\eta\Omega)\,u+\sin(\eta\Omega)\,e(u,v),&c<-1+\epsilon_{\Omega},\\[2.0pt] \Slerp_{\eta}(u,v),&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (12)

The last branch is the exact step, and the middle one makes the unavoidable choice of arc near an antipode explicit. The first branch is what the solver executes in the convergence regime, and the following lemma is what the boundedness argument of Section 3.2.1 needs from it.

Lemma 2 (The guarded step stays on the sphere and on the arc).

Let u,v∈𝕊d−1u,v\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1} and η∈[0,1]\eta\in[0,1]. Every branch of eq. 12 returns a unit vector. On the first branch, nlerpη⁡(u,v)\nlerp_{\eta}(u,v) lies on the same great circle as Slerpη⁡(u,v)\Slerp_{\eta}(u,v), at angle θ=η​Ω+O⁡(Ω3)\theta=\eta\Omega+O(\Omega^{3}) from uu, where Ω=∠⁡(u,v)\Omega=\angle(u,v).

Proof.

The first branch normalizes explicitly, the third has unit norm by Lemma 1, and the middle branch is cos⁡(η​Ω)​u+sin⁡(η​Ω)​e\cos(\eta\Omega)u+\sin(\eta\Omega)e with e⟂ue\perp u of unit norm. For the first branch, (1−η)​u+η​v(1-\eta)u+\eta v lies in span​{u,v}\mathrm{span}\{u,v\}, so normalizing it lands on the great circle through uu and vv: the guard can change the position along the arc, not the arc. Its angle θ\theta from uu satisfies

cos⁡θ=(1−η)+η​cos⁡Ω∥(1−η)​u+η​v∥2=1−η​Ω2/2+O⁡(Ω4)1−η⁡(1−η)​Ω2/2+O⁡(Ω4)=1−η2​Ω22+O⁡(Ω4),\cos\theta=\frac{(1-\eta)+\eta\cos\Omega}{\lVert(1-\eta)u+\eta v\rVert_{2}}=\frac{1-\eta\Omega^{2}/2+O(\Omega^{4})}{1-\eta(1-\eta)\Omega^{2}/2+O(\Omega^{4})}=1-\frac{\eta^{2}\Omega^{2}}{2}+O(\Omega^{4}),

using cos⁡Ω=1−Ω2/2+O⁡(Ω4)\cos\Omega=1-\Omega^{2}/2+O(\Omega^{4}) and ∥(1−η)​u+η​v∥22=1−2​η​(1−η)​(1−cos⁡Ω)\lVert(1-\eta)u+\eta v\rVert_{2}^{2}=1-2\eta(1-\eta)(1-\cos\Omega). Hence θ=η​Ω+O⁡(Ω3)\theta=\eta\Omega+O(\Omega^{3}): the guard’s error is a third-order timing error along the correct arc. The guard fires for Ω≲2​ϵΩ\Omega\lesssim\sqrt{2\epsilon_{\Omega}}, where this discrepancy is of order ϵΩ3/2\epsilon_{\Omega}^{3/2}, while the 0/00/0 is removed. ∎

A.3 Euclidean mixing follows the same geodesic

This is the identity behind the geodesic injection of eq. 8: FPRM’s affine input mixing, once normalized, moves along the same arc with a state-dependent fraction.

Lemma 3 (Normalized Euclidean mixing follows the same geodesic).

Let u,v∈ℝd∖{0}u,v\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus\{0\}, write u^=u/∥u∥2\widehat{u}=u/\lVert u\rVert_{2} and v^=v/∥v∥2\widehat{v}=v/\lVert v\rVert_{2}, and assume v^≠−u^\widehat{v}\neq-\widehat{u}. For any α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0, if Ω=∠⁡(u^,v^)∈(0,π)\Omega=\angle(\widehat{u},\widehat{v})\in(0,\pi), then

Norm⁡(α​u+β​v)\displaystyle\Norm(\alpha u+\beta v) =Slerpλeff⁡(u^,v^),\displaystyle=\Slerp_{\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}}}(\widehat{u},\widehat{v}), (13)
λeff\displaystyle\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}} =1Ω​atan2⁡(β​∥v∥2​sin⁡Ω,α​∥u∥2+β​∥v∥2​cos⁡Ω)∈(0,1).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\Omega}\operatorname{atan2}\!\left(\beta\lVert v\rVert_{2}\sin\Omega,\;\alpha\lVert u\rVert_{2}+\beta\lVert v\rVert_{2}\cos\Omega\right)\in(0,1).

If Ω=0\Omega=0, then Norm⁡(α​u+β​v)=u^=v^\Norm(\alpha u+\beta v)=\widehat{u}=\widehat{v}.

Proof.

If Ω=0\Omega=0, then u^=v^\widehat{u}=\widehat{v} and the positive mixture α​u+β​v=(α​∥u∥2+β​∥v∥2)​u^\alpha u+\beta v=(\alpha\lVert u\rVert_{2}+\beta\lVert v\rVert_{2})\widehat{u} normalizes to u^\widehat{u}. This is also Slerps⁡(u^,u^)\Slerp_{s}(\widehat{u},\widehat{u}) for every s∈[0,1]s\in[0,1].

For 0<Ω<π0<\Omega<\pi, define

e:=v^−cos⁡Ω​u^sin⁡Ω.e:=\frac{\widehat{v}-\cos\Omega\,\widehat{u}}{\sin\Omega}.

As in Lemma 1, u^\widehat{u} and ee are orthonormal and v^=cos⁡Ω​u^+sin⁡Ω​e\widehat{v}=\cos\Omega\,\widehat{u}+\sin\Omega\,e. Hence

α​u+β​v=(α​∥u∥2+β​∥v∥2​cos⁡Ω)​u^+β​∥v∥2​sin⁡Ω​e.\alpha u+\beta v=\left(\alpha\lVert u\rVert_{2}+\beta\lVert v\rVert_{2}\cos\Omega\right)\widehat{u}+\beta\lVert v\rVert_{2}\sin\Omega\,e.

By the definition of atan2\operatorname{atan2} and λeff\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}} in the lemma, the normalized mixture is therefore

Norm⁡(α​u+β​v)=cos⁡(λeff​Ω)​u^+sin⁡(λeff​Ω)​e.\Norm(\alpha u+\beta v)=\cos(\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}}\Omega)\,\widehat{u}+\sin(\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}}\Omega)\,e.

The first argument of atan2\operatorname{atan2} is positive, so 0<λeff​Ω<π0<\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}}\Omega<\pi. Moreover,

sin⁡(Ω−λeff​Ω)=α​∥u∥2​sin⁡Ω∥α​u+β​v∥2>0.\sin\!\left(\Omega-\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}}\Omega\right)=\frac{\alpha\lVert u\rVert_{2}\sin\Omega}{\lVert\alpha u+\beta v\rVert_{2}}>0.

Since Ω−λeff​Ω∈(−π,π)\Omega-\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}}\Omega\in(-\pi,\pi), this implies 0<λeff​Ω<Ω0<\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}}\Omega<\Omega, or 0<λeff<10<\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}}<1. The representation in Lemma 1 now gives

Norm⁡(α​u+β​v)=Slerpλeff⁡(u^,v^),\Norm(\alpha u+\beta v)=\Slerp_{\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}}}\!\left(\widehat{u},\widehat{v}\right),

which is exactly eq. 13.

At Ω=π\Omega=\pi, the shortest great-circle direction is not unique. If the two opposing weighted vectors also have equal magnitudes, their Euclidean mixture is zero and cannot be normalized. This explains why antipodal directions are excluded. ∎

A.4 Detailed proof of fixed-point existence

Proof of Proposition 1.

Set R:=(1−λ)​πR:=(1-\lambda)\pi. Since 0<λ<10<\lambda<1, we have 0<R<π0<R<\pi. Recall the cap

𝒞𝐱={𝐲∈𝒮:∠⁡(yt,xt)≤R​ for every ​t}.\mathcal{C}_{\mathbf{x}}=\left\{\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{S}:\angle(y_{t},x_{t})\leq R\text{ for every }t\right\}.

The exact recurrent map FθF_{\theta} does not generally map this cap into itself, because the network is applied after the token-wise interpolation in eq. 8. The proof therefore uses the reversed order only in an auxiliary map:

H⁡(𝐲):=Slerpλ⁡(fθ​(𝐲),𝐱).H(\mathbf{y}):=\Slerp_{\lambda}\!\left(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}),\mathbf{x}\right).

For every 𝐲∈𝒞𝐱\mathbf{y}\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathbf{x}}, the assumptions ensure that fθ​(𝐲)tf_{\theta}(\mathbf{y})_{t} is a unit vector different from −xt-x_{t}. By Lemma 1,

∠⁡(H​(𝐲)t,xt)\displaystyle\angle\!\left(H(\mathbf{y})_{t},x_{t}\right) =(1−λ)​∠​(fθ​(𝐲)t,xt)\displaystyle=(1-\lambda)\angle\!\left(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{y})_{t},x_{t}\right)
<(1−λ)​π=R.\displaystyle<(1-\lambda)\pi=R.

Thus H⁡(𝒞𝐱)⊆𝒞𝐱H(\mathcal{C}_{\mathbf{x}})\subseteq\mathcal{C}_{\mathbf{x}}. Continuity of fθf_{\theta} and exclusion of the antipode make HH continuous throughout this cap.

We next give the Euclidean coordinates needed for Brouwer’s theorem. The spherical logarithm below is a vector-valued coordinate map, not a scalar logarithm. Given unit vectors uu and v≠−uv\neq-u, let Ω=∠⁡(u,v)<π\Omega=\angle(u,v)<\pi and define

Logu⁡(v):={0,v=u,Ωsin⁡Ω​(v−cos⁡Ω​u),v≠u.\Log_{u}(v):=\begin{cases}0,&v=u,\\[2.0pt] \displaystyle\frac{\Omega}{\sin\Omega}\left(v-\cos\Omega\,u\right),&v\neq u.\end{cases}

The vector in parentheses is orthogonal to uu and has norm sin⁡Ω\sin\Omega. Therefore

⟨Logu⁡(v),u⟩=0,∥Logu⁡(v)∥2=Ω.\langle\Log_{u}(v),\,u\rangle=0,\qquad\lVert\Log_{u}(v)\rVert_{2}=\Omega.

In words, Logu⁡(v)\Log_{u}(v) points in the tangent direction of the shortest arc from uu to vv, and its length equals that arc’s angle. Its inverse is

Expu⁡(w):={u,w=0,cos⁡(∥w∥2)​u+sin⁡(∥w∥2)​w∥w∥2,w≠0,\Exp_{u}(w):=\begin{cases}u,&w=0,\\[2.0pt] \displaystyle\cos(\lVert w\rVert_{2})u+\sin(\lVert w\rVert_{2})\frac{w}{\lVert w\rVert_{2}},&w\neq 0,\end{cases}

for ⟨w,u⟩=0\langle w,\,u\rangle=0 and ∥w∥2<π\lVert w\rVert_{2}<\pi. The two maps are continuous inverses on every closed cap of radius strictly smaller than π\pi.

Applying the spherical logarithm token by token identifies 𝒞𝐱\mathcal{C}_{\mathbf{x}} continuously and bijectively with

ℬ:=∏t=1T{ut∈ℝd:⟨ut,xt⟩=0,∥ut∥2≤R}.\mathcal{B}:=\prod_{t=1}^{T}\left\{u_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\langle u_{t},\,x_{t}\rangle=0,\ \lVert u_{t}\rVert_{2}\leq R\right\}.

Each factor is an ordinary closed Euclidean ball inside the hyperplane perpendicular to xtx_{t}. Consequently, ℬ\mathcal{B} is nonempty, compact, and convex and can be identified with a subset of ℝT⁡(d−1)\mathbb{R}^{T(d-1)}.

We now apply Brouwer’s fixed-point theorem (Brouwer, 1911), in the following standard form: if KK is a nonempty, compact, convex subset of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space and G:K→KG:K\to K is continuous, then

there exists ​y⋆∈K​ such that ​G​(y⋆)=y⋆.\text{there exists }y^{\star}\in K\text{ such that }G(y^{\star})=y^{\star}.

For a textbook statement, see Ortega and Rheinboldt (1970, Section 6.3, p. 161). Transforming HH into the logarithmic coordinates above produces just such a continuous self-map of ℬ\mathcal{B}. Therefore there exists 𝐲⋆∈𝒞𝐱\mathbf{y}^{\star}\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathbf{x}} such that

𝐲⋆=H⁡(𝐲⋆)=Slerpλ⁡(fθ​(𝐲⋆),𝐱).\mathbf{y}^{\star}=H(\mathbf{y}^{\star})=\Slerp_{\lambda}\!\left(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}^{\star}),\mathbf{x}\right).

Now define

𝐳⋆:=fθ​(𝐲⋆).\mathbf{z}^{\star}:=f_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}^{\star}).

The preceding fixed-point identity gives 𝐲⋆=Slerpλ⁡(𝐳⋆,𝐱)\mathbf{y}^{\star}=\Slerp_{\lambda}(\mathbf{z}^{\star},\mathbf{x}), and hence

Fθ​(𝐳⋆,𝐱)\displaystyle F_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}^{\star};\mathbf{x}) =fθ​(Slerpλ⁡(𝐳⋆,𝐱))\displaystyle=f_{\theta}\!\left(\Slerp_{\lambda}(\mathbf{z}^{\star},\mathbf{x})\right)
=fθ​(𝐲⋆)=𝐳⋆.\displaystyle=f_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}^{\star})=\mathbf{z}^{\star}.

Thus 𝐳⋆\mathbf{z}^{\star} is a fixed point of the exact injection-first recurrent map. Notice that the proof places 𝐲⋆\mathbf{y}^{\star}, not necessarily 𝐳⋆\mathbf{z}^{\star}, in the input-centered cap. ∎

A.5 The first derivative of slerp at coincident endpoints

Lemma 4 (First-order interpolation rule).

Fix 0≤η≤10\leq\eta\leq 1 and a∈𝕊d−1a\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}. As unit vectors u,vu,v approach aa,

Slerpη⁡(u,v)=(1−η)​u+η​v+O⁡(∥u−v∥22),\Slerp_{\eta}(u,v)=(1-\eta)u+\eta v+O(\lVert u-v\rVert_{2}^{2}),

with the exact value Slerpη⁡(u,u)=u\Slerp_{\eta}(u,u)=u at coincidence. In particular, the interpolation is jointly differentiable at (a,a)(a,a), with tangent derivative

D​Slerpη⁡(a,a)​[h,k]=(1−η)​h+η​k,⟨a,h⟩=⟨a,k⟩=0.D\Slerp_{\eta}(a,a)[h,k]=(1-\eta)h+\eta k,\qquad\langle a,\,h\rangle=\langle a,\,k\rangle=0.
Proof.

For Ω=∠⁡(u,v)>0\Omega=\angle(u,v)>0 small, the elementary estimate sin⁡(c​Ω)=c​Ω+O⁡(Ω3)\sin(c\Omega)=c\Omega+O(\Omega^{3}), for fixed cc, gives

sin⁡((1−η)​Ω)sin⁡Ω=(1−η)+O⁡(Ω2),sin⁡(η​Ω)sin⁡Ω=η+O⁡(Ω2).\frac{\sin((1-\eta)\Omega)}{\sin\Omega}=(1-\eta)+O(\Omega^{2}),\qquad\frac{\sin(\eta\Omega)}{\sin\Omega}=\eta+O(\Omega^{2}).

Substituting into the interpolation formula gives an error of order Ω2\Omega^{2}, since both endpoints have unit norm. The chord identity ∥u−v∥2=2​sin⁡(Ω/2)\lVert u-v\rVert_{2}=2\sin(\Omega/2) implies Ω=O⁡(∥u−v∥2)\Omega=O(\lVert u-v\rVert_{2}), proving the stated estimate. If u=vu=v, the error is exactly zero because Slerpη⁡(u,u)=u\Slerp_{\eta}(u,u)=u.

To obtain the joint derivative, express nearby endpoints using tangent coordinates h,k⟂ah,k\perp a:

u=a+h∥a+h∥2=a+h+O⁡(∥h∥22),v=a+k∥a+k∥2=a+k+O⁡(∥k∥22).u=\frac{a+h}{\lVert a+h\rVert_{2}}=a+h+O(\lVert h\rVert_{2}^{2}),\qquad v=\frac{a+k}{\lVert a+k\rVert_{2}}=a+k+O(\lVert k\rVert_{2}^{2}).

Here ∥a+h∥22=1+∥h∥22\lVert a+h\rVert_{2}^{2}=1+\lVert h\rVert_{2}^{2}, so normalization has no first-order effect. The uniform interpolation estimate now yields

Slerpη⁡(u,v)=a+(1−η)​h+η​k+O⁡(∥h∥22+∥k∥22).\Slerp_{\eta}(u,v)=a+(1-\eta)h+\eta k+O(\lVert h\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lVert k\rVert_{2}^{2}).

Thus the linear response to arbitrary simultaneous endpoint perturbations is (1−η)​h+η​k(1-\eta)h+\eta k, as claimed. ∎

A.6 Proof of local convergence under angular damping

Proof of Theorem 1.

Tangent directions and fixed points. Let J=D𝐳​Fθ​(𝐳⋆,𝐱)J=D_{\mathbf{z}}F_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}^{\star};\mathbf{x}). Consider a differentiable spherical curve 𝐳⁡(ε)\mathbf{z}(\varepsilon) with 𝐳⁡(0)=𝐳⋆\mathbf{z}(0)=\mathbf{z}^{\star} and 𝐳′​(0)=𝐮\mathbf{z}^{\prime}(0)=\mathbf{u}. Both its input and output tokens have unit norm, so differentiation gives

0\displaystyle 0 =dd​ε​∥zt​(ε)∥22|ε=0=2​⟨zt⋆,ut⟩,\displaystyle=\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\lVert z_{t}(\varepsilon)\rVert_{2}^{2}\right|_{\varepsilon=0}=2\langle z_{t}^{\star},\,u_{t}\rangle,
0\displaystyle 0 =dd​ε​∥Fθ​(𝐳⁡(ε),𝐱)t∥22|ε=0=2​⟨zt⋆,(J​𝐮)t⟩.\displaystyle=\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\lVert F_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}(\varepsilon);\mathbf{x})_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}\right|_{\varepsilon=0}=2\langle z_{t}^{\star},\,(J\mathbf{u})_{t}\rangle.

The output derivative uses Fθ​(𝐳⋆,𝐱)=𝐳⋆F_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}^{\star};\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{z}^{\star}. Hence JJ sends tangent perturbations to tangent perturbations at the same fixed point; it includes all coupling between tokens.

For η>0\eta>0, interpolation moves a positive fraction of the shortest arc, so it returns its first endpoint exactly when the endpoints coincide. The damped update therefore has exactly the fixed points of FθF_{\theta}, wherever these arcs are defined. At 𝐳⋆\mathbf{z}^{\star} the endpoints coincide, and continuity ensures that nearby endpoint pairs are non-antipodal.

Linearization and the damping range.

Represent a nearby state by tangent coordinates 𝐰=(wt)t=1T\mathbf{w}=(w_{t})_{t=1}^{T}:

zt=zt⋆+wt∥zt⋆+wt∥2,⟨zt⋆,wt⟩=0.z_{t}=\frac{z_{t}^{\star}+w_{t}}{\lVert z_{t}^{\star}+w_{t}\rVert_{2}},\qquad\langle z_{t}^{\star},\,w_{t}\rangle=0.

These coordinates measure displacement along the sphere to first order: 𝐳=𝐳⋆+𝐰+O⁡(∥𝐰∥2)\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{z}^{\star}+\mathbf{w}+O(\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^{2}). The inverse is wt=zt/⟨zt⋆,zt⟩−zt⋆w_{t}=z_{t}/\langle z_{t}^{\star},\,z_{t}\rangle-z_{t}^{\star}, defined nearby, and also has identity tangent derivative. Differentiability of FθF_{\theta} gives

Fθ​(𝐳,𝐱)=𝐳⋆+J​𝐰+o⁡(∥𝐰∥).F_{\theta}(\mathbf{z};\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{z}^{\star}+J\mathbf{w}+o(\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert).

In particular, the two interpolation endpoints differ by O⁡(∥𝐰∥)O(\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert). By Lemma 4, replacing their spherical interpolation by their weighted average incurs only O⁡(∥𝐰∥2)O(\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^{2}) error. Thus, writing Φη\Phi_{\eta} for the damped update in these coordinates,

Φη​(𝐰)=A​𝐰+o⁡(∥𝐰∥),A:=(1−η)​Id+η​J.\Phi_{\eta}(\mathbf{w})=A\mathbf{w}+o(\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert),\qquad A:=(1-\eta)\operatorname{Id}+\eta J.

If J​v=ζ​vJv=\zeta v for a nonzero, possibly complex eigenvector vv, then A​v=[1+η⁡(ζ−1)]​vAv=[1+\eta(\zeta-1)]v. Conversely, every eigenvector of AA is one of J=(A−(1−η)​Id)/ηJ=(A-(1-\eta)\operatorname{Id})/\eta. This identifies all eigenvalues without assuming diagonalizability. As in Euclidean damping (Movahedi et al., 2026, Appendix A.3),

|1+η⁡(ζ−1)|2=1+2​η​(Re⁡(ζ)−1)+η2​|ζ−1|2<1|1+\eta(\zeta-1)|^{2}=1+2\eta(\Real(\zeta)-1)+\eta^{2}|\zeta-1|^{2}<1

exactly when 0<η<2​(1−Re⁡(ζ))/|ζ−1|20<\eta<2(1-\Real(\zeta))/|\zeta-1|^{2}. The theorem’s damping bound therefore places every eigenvalue of AA strictly inside the unit disk.

From the linearization to convergence.

This eigenvalue condition need not make the Euclidean norm shrink at every step. A standard finite-dimensional stability result instead provides a vector norm ∥⋅∥∗\lVert\cdot\rVert_{*} with induced matrix norm a:=∥A∥∗<1a:=\lVert A\rVert_{*}<1 (Ortega and Rheinboldt, 1970). This norm is equivalent to the Euclidean norm: positive constants c1,c2c_{1},c_{2} satisfy

c1​∥𝐰∥≤∥𝐰∥∗≤c2​∥𝐰∥.c_{1}\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert\leq\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_{*}\leq c_{2}\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert.

It therefore measures the same notion of convergence, up to fixed factors.

Choose a<q<1a<q<1. The remainder o⁡(∥𝐰∥)o(\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert) means that its norm divided by ∥𝐰∥\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert tends to zero. By norm equivalence, we may choose a sufficiently small neighborhood where

∥Φη​(𝐰)−A​𝐰∥∗≤(q−a)​∥𝐰∥∗.\lVert\Phi_{\eta}(\mathbf{w})-A\mathbf{w}\rVert_{*}\leq(q-a)\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_{*}.

The triangle inequality then gives the full one-step error bound:

∥Φη​(𝐰)∥∗\displaystyle\lVert\Phi_{\eta}(\mathbf{w})\rVert_{*} ≤∥A​𝐰∥∗+∥Φη​(𝐰)−A​𝐰∥∗\displaystyle\leq\lVert A\mathbf{w}\rVert_{*}+\lVert\Phi_{\eta}(\mathbf{w})-A\mathbf{w}\rVert_{*}
≤a​∥𝐰∥∗+(q−a)​∥𝐰∥∗=q​∥𝐰∥∗.\displaystyle\leq a\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_{*}+(q-a)\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_{*}=q\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_{*}.

Because q<1q<1, a sufficiently small ball in this norm stays within itself after every update. Starting there, induction gives ∥𝐰i∥∗≤qi​∥𝐰0∥∗\lVert\mathbf{w}_{i}\rVert_{*}\leq q^{i}\lVert\mathbf{w}_{0}\rVert_{*}. Finally, the coordinate map and its inverse are smooth nearby, so they bound coordinate error and state error by constant multiples of each other. Together with norm equivalence, this yields

∥𝐳i−𝐳⋆∥≤C​qi​∥𝐳0−𝐳⋆∥\lVert\mathbf{z}_{i}-\mathbf{z}^{\star}\rVert\leq Cq^{i}\lVert\mathbf{z}_{0}-\mathbf{z}^{\star}\rVert

for some C>0C>0, proving the asserted local geometric convergence. ∎

The guarded step.

Near 𝐳⋆\mathbf{z}^{\star} the endpoints 𝐳i\mathbf{z}_{i} and Fθ​(𝐳i,𝐱)F_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{i};\mathbf{x}) are O⁡(∥𝐰∥)O(\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert) apart, so on a neighborhood of 𝐳⋆\mathbf{z}^{\star} the solver executes the first branch of eq. 12. By Lemma 2 that branch lies on the same arc as the exact step, at an angle from uu that differs by O⁡(Ω3)O(\Omega^{3}), so it differs from Slerpη⁡(u,v)\Slerp_{\eta}(u,v) by O⁡(∥u−v∥23)O(\lVert u-v\rVert_{2}^{3}) and shares the expansion (1−η)​u+η​v+O⁡(∥u−v∥22)(1-\eta)u+\eta v+O(\lVert u-v\rVert_{2}^{2}) of Lemma 4. It also returns uu only when v=uv=u, because for η>0\eta>0 a normalized nonnegative combination of two non-antipodal unit vectors equals uu only if v=uv=u. The proof above therefore applies verbatim, and Theorem 1 holds for the guarded step the solver runs.

Remark 1 (Optimal damping, and when the window is narrow).

Write ζ=a+b​i\zeta=a+bi. The squared modulus |1+η⁡(ζ−1)|2=1−2​η​(1−a)+η2​|ζ−1|2|1+\eta(\zeta-1)|^{2}=1-2\eta(1-a)+\eta^{2}|\zeta-1|^{2} is an upward parabola in η\eta with value 11 at η=0\eta=0, so for a<1a<1 the window 0<η<2​(1−a)/|ζ−1|20<\eta<2(1-a)/|\zeta-1|^{2} of eq. 11 is exactly the interval on which it lies below one, the vertex η⋆=(1−a)/|ζ−1|2\eta^{\star}=(1-a)/|\zeta-1|^{2} is the optimal damping for that mode, and the smallest attainable squared modulus is 1−(1−a)2/|ζ−1|21-(1-a)^{2}/|\zeta-1|^{2}, a contraction factor of 1−(1−a)2/|ζ−1|2\sqrt{1-(1-a)^{2}/|\zeta-1|^{2}} per step. Three consequences. (i) Damping handles rotation but not expansion: for a≥1a\geq 1 every term is nonnegative, so no η>0\eta>0 contracts the mode and only training can remove it. (ii) The guarantee is weak when 1−a1-a is small compared with |b||b|, that is, when ζ−1\zeta-1 is nearly imaginary, whatever |ζ||\zeta| is: for ζ=0.9+1.5​i\zeta=0.9+1.5i the undamped mode grows by |ζ|≈1.75|\zeta|\approx 1.75 per step while rotating by about 59∘59^{\circ}, the window is 0<η<0.0890<\eta<0.089, and even the optimal damping contracts by only 0.22%0.22\% per step, so halving the error takes about 313313 iterations. Bounding the rotation magnitude, not only the expansion, is therefore what makes halting fast. (iii) The patience rule of Algorithm 1, which starts at η=1\eta=1 and multiplies it by γ\gamma whenever the residual stalls, is a derivative-free descent into this window: well-conditioned modes (ζ=0.5\zeta=0.5 admits every η<4\eta<4) converge at once, and the geometric decay eventually drops η\eta below the threshold of the rotational modes, at which point their tangent error contracts geometrically and, whenever the residual then improves within PP iterations, the decay pauses, without any spectrum ever being estimated. Because the contraction is in an adapted norm, the residual need not fall monotonically, so the rule may keep shrinking η\eta; this slows convergence but cannot break it, since every smaller η\eta stays inside the window.

A.7 Global convergence under sufficiently strong input injection

Proof of Theorem 2.

We use the token-wise logarithm and exponential from Appendix A.4. They satisfy

Slerpλ⁡(𝐳,𝐱)=Exp𝐱⁡((1−λ)​Log𝐱⁡(𝐳))\Slerp_{\lambda}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{x})=\Exp_{\mathbf{x}}\!\left((1-\lambda)\Log_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{z})\right)

whenever zt≠−xtz_{t}\neq-x_{t} for every token tt. Indeed, eq. 6 gives Slerpλ⁡(zt,xt)=Slerp1−λ⁡(xt,zt)\Slerp_{\lambda}(z_{t},x_{t})=\Slerp_{1-\lambda}(x_{t},z_{t}), which by the representation in Lemma 1 equals cos⁡((1−λ)​Ω)​xt+sin⁡((1−λ)​Ω)​e\cos((1-\lambda)\Omega)\,x_{t}+\sin((1-\lambda)\Omega)\,e with Ω=∠⁡(xt,zt)\Omega=\angle(x_{t},z_{t}) and Logxt⁡(zt)=Ω​e\Log_{x_{t}}(z_{t})=\Omega e, and this is Expxt⁡((1−λ)​Logxt⁡(zt))\Exp_{x_{t}}((1-\lambda)\Log_{x_{t}}(z_{t})) by definition, also when Ω=0\Omega=0. Thus input injection multiplies the logarithmic coordinates by exactly 1−λ1-\lambda: it preserves the direction toward the current state while reducing its angular distance from the input.

The geometric difficulty is that shrinking angles to the input does not give a global contraction bound between states. Two states approaching an input antipode along different arcs can be arbitrarily close while their injected states remain separated for fixed 0<λ<10<\lambda<1. Thus the direct global Lipschitz argument for Euclidean input mixing in FPRM (Movahedi et al., 2026, Appendix A.2) does not apply here. Instead, every injected token has angle less than (1−λ)​π(1-\lambda)\pi to its input. We use this uniform bound to place all injected states in one fixed neighborhood, prove contraction in its logarithmic coordinates, and then transfer convergence back to the original states.

These are smooth inverse coordinate maps for ∥wt∥2<π\lVert w_{t}\rVert_{2}<\pi. The spherical exponential is smooth, and its differential has singular values 11 in the radial direction and sin⁡r/r\sin r/r in the transverse directions at radius 0<r<π0<r<\pi, with identity differential at the origin. Its differential is therefore invertible throughout this domain, so the inverse function theorem gives smoothness of the logarithm.

A fixed neighborhood of the input.

Since fθf_{\theta} is C1C^{1} near 𝐱\mathbf{x} and fθ​(𝐱)t≠−xtf_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})_{t}\neq-x_{t} for every tt, continuity allows us to choose 0<r<π/20<r<\pi/2 such that fθ∘Exp𝐱f_{\theta}\circ\Exp_{\mathbf{x}} is C1C^{1} and none of its output tokens equals −xt-x_{t} on an open neighborhood of

ℬr:={𝐰∈(ℝd)T:⟨wt,xt⟩=0,∥wt∥2≤r for every t}.\mathcal{B}_{r}:=\left\{\mathbf{w}\in(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{T}:\langle w_{t},\,x_{t}\rangle=0,\quad\lVert w_{t}\rVert_{2}\leq r\text{ for every }t\right\}.

Here ℬr\mathcal{B}_{r} is a compact, convex product of ordinary tangent-space balls. Define, on this neighborhood,

A⁡(𝐰):=Log𝐱⁡(fθ​(Exp𝐱⁡(𝐰))).A(\mathbf{w}):=\Log_{\mathbf{x}}\!\left(f_{\theta}(\Exp_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{w}))\right).

Here 𝐰\mathbf{w} represents an injected state, and A⁡(𝐰)A(\mathbf{w}) represents the network’s output in the same coordinates. Multiplication by 1−λ1-\lambda then performs the next input injection. Both AA and fθ∘Exp𝐱f_{\theta}\circ\Exp_{\mathbf{x}} are C1C^{1}, so their derivatives are bounded on the compact set ℬr\mathcal{B}_{r}. Integrating these derivatives along the line segment between any 𝐰,𝐯∈ℬr\mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}\in\mathcal{B}_{r} gives a common finite constant L≥1L\geq 1 such that

∥A⁡(𝐰)−A⁡(𝐯)∥\displaystyle\lVert A(\mathbf{w})-A(\mathbf{v})\rVert ≤L​∥𝐰−𝐯∥,\displaystyle\leq L\lVert\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{v}\rVert,
∥fθ​(Exp𝐱⁡(𝐰))−fθ​(Exp𝐱⁡(𝐯))∥\displaystyle\lVert f_{\theta}(\Exp_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{w}))-f_{\theta}(\Exp_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{v}))\rVert ≤L​∥𝐰−𝐯∥.\displaystyle\leq L\lVert\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{v}\rVert.

All norms here are the product Euclidean norm defined in the main text. Moreover, ∥A​(𝐰)t∥2<π\lVert A(\mathbf{w})_{t}\rVert_{2}<\pi for every token, because the logarithm’s length is the angle to xtx_{t} and the antipode is excluded.

Strong injection gives a contraction.

Choose

λ0:=1−min⁡{rπ,12​L}∈(0,1).\lambda_{0}:=1-\min\!\left\{\frac{r}{\pi},\frac{1}{2L}\right\}\in(0,1).

Fix any λ∈(λ0,1)\lambda\in(\lambda_{0},1), and set a:=1−λa:=1-\lambda and q:=a​Lq:=aL. Then a​π<ra\pi<r and 0<q<1/20<q<1/2. The two terms in the threshold serve separate purposes: a​π<ra\pi<r keeps all injected states in the chosen neighborhood, while a​L<1aL<1 makes their distances contract. The factor 1/21/2 simply leaves a strict margin below one. The map 𝐰↦a​A​(𝐰)\mathbf{w}\mapsto aA(\mathbf{w}) sends ℬr\mathcal{B}_{r} into itself, since

∥a​A​(𝐰)t∥2<a​π<r.\lVert aA(\mathbf{w})_{t}\rVert_{2}<a\pi<r.

It is also a contraction:

∥a​A​(𝐰)−a​A​(𝐯)∥≤q⁡∥𝐰−𝐯∥.\lVert aA(\mathbf{w})-aA(\mathbf{v})\rVert\leq q\lVert\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{v}\rVert.

The set ℬr\mathcal{B}_{r} is closed in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, hence complete. Banach’s contraction theorem therefore gives a unique 𝐰⋆∈ℬr\mathbf{w}^{\star}\in\mathcal{B}_{r} satisfying 𝐰⋆=a​A​(𝐰⋆)\mathbf{w}^{\star}=aA(\mathbf{w}^{\star}), and every iteration 𝐰i+1=a​A​(𝐰i)\mathbf{w}_{i+1}=aA(\mathbf{w}_{i}) starting in ℬr\mathcal{B}_{r} satisfies

∥𝐰i−𝐰⋆∥≤qi​∥𝐰0−𝐰⋆∥.\lVert\mathbf{w}_{i}-\mathbf{w}^{\star}\rVert\leq q^{i}\lVert\mathbf{w}_{0}-\mathbf{w}^{\star}\rVert.
Return to the original recurrence.

Let 𝐳0\mathbf{z}_{0} be any admissible initialization, with z0,t≠−xtz_{0,t}\neq-x_{t} for every tt, and set

𝐰0:=a​Log𝐱⁡(𝐳0).\mathbf{w}_{0}:=a\Log_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{z}_{0}).

Because ∥w0,t∥2<a​π<r\lVert w_{0,t}\rVert_{2}<a\pi<r, this initial coordinate lies in ℬr\mathcal{B}_{r}, regardless of the distance from 𝐳0\mathbf{z}_{0} to a fixed point. The original recurrence and the coordinate iteration are related by

𝐳i+1=fθ​(Exp𝐱⁡(𝐰i)),𝐰i+1=a​Log𝐱⁡(𝐳i+1)=a​A​(𝐰i).\mathbf{z}_{i+1}=f_{\theta}(\Exp_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{w}_{i})),\qquad\mathbf{w}_{i+1}=a\Log_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{z}_{i+1})=aA(\mathbf{w}_{i}).

These identities hold inductively for every i≥0i\geq 0: each 𝐰i\mathbf{w}_{i} remains in ℬr\mathcal{B}_{r}, where the network’s outputs avoid the antipodes. Hence every subsequent interpolation is well-defined.

Define 𝐳⋆:=fθ​(Exp𝐱⁡(𝐰⋆))\mathbf{z}^{\star}:=f_{\theta}(\Exp_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{w}^{\star})). The identity 𝐰⋆=a​A​(𝐰⋆)\mathbf{w}^{\star}=aA(\mathbf{w}^{\star}) implies 𝐰⋆=a​Log𝐱⁡(𝐳⋆)\mathbf{w}^{\star}=a\Log_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{z}^{\star}), so

Fθ​(𝐳⋆,𝐱)=fθ​(Exp𝐱⁡(𝐰⋆))=𝐳⋆.F_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}^{\star};\mathbf{x})=f_{\theta}(\Exp_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{w}^{\star}))=\mathbf{z}^{\star}.

This fixed point is admissible by the choice of rr. Conversely, any admissible fixed point 𝐳\mathbf{z} of FθF_{\theta} gives 𝐰=a​Log𝐱⁡(𝐳)∈ℬr\mathbf{w}=a\Log_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{z})\in\mathcal{B}_{r} with 𝐰=a​A​(𝐰)\mathbf{w}=aA(\mathbf{w}). Uniqueness of 𝐰⋆\mathbf{w}^{\star} then implies 𝐳=𝐳⋆\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{z}^{\star}.

Finally, the Lipschitz bound above transfers convergence to the original states:

∥𝐳i+1−𝐳⋆∥\displaystyle\lVert\mathbf{z}_{i+1}-\mathbf{z}^{\star}\rVert ≤L⁡∥𝐰i−𝐰⋆∥\displaystyle\leq L\lVert\mathbf{w}_{i}-\mathbf{w}^{\star}\rVert
≤L​qi​∥𝐰0−𝐰⋆∥≤2​L​r​T​qi,i≥0.\displaystyle\leq Lq^{i}\lVert\mathbf{w}_{0}-\mathbf{w}^{\star}\rVert\leq 2Lr\sqrt{T}\,q^{i},\qquad i\geq 0.

Thus the theorem holds with C=2​L​r​TC=2Lr\sqrt{T}, uniformly over all admissible initializations. The neighborhood, derivative bound, and injection threshold depend on the fixed network and input. ∎

Appendix B Details on Experimental Setup

This appendix section provides the details on the experimental setup and experiments in Section 4. Details on tasks and data are in Appendix B.1, on models in Appendix B.2, on training and solver settings in Appendix B.3. Table 3 reports all hyperparameters. The evaluation protocol is in Appendix B.4.

B.1 Tasks and data

Sudoku-Extreme. This dataset consists of 9×99{\times}9 Sudoku puzzles selected for difficulty, with a test split of 422,786422{,}786 puzzles. The standard training build has 1,0001{,}000 base puzzles, each augmented 1000×1000\times by validity-preserving transformations (relabeling of the digits and permutations of rows, columns, bands, and stacks), giving 10610^{6} training examples. We train instead on a 55k×200\times 200 build, 5,0005{,}000 base puzzles with 200200 augmentations each, which has the same number of training examples. Unless stated otherwise, every SFPRM Sudoku run and every rollout of Sections 4.2 and 4.3 uses this build. A puzzle is a sequence of 8181 cell tokens (blank or a digit) preceded by a learned per-puzzle embedding of 1616 tokens, and the model predicts the digit of every cell.

Maze-Hard. The 30×3030{\times}30 maze benchmark of the same suite: 1,0001{,}000 training and 1,0001{,}000 test mazes, used without augmentation. A maze is a sequence of 900900 cell tokens (wall, free, start, goal) plus the puzzle embedding, and the model predicts for every cell whether it lies on the shortest path.

Mini-ARC. A 5×55{\times}5-grid ARC variant (Kim et al., 2022) with 149149 tasks. We train on the 528528 demonstration pairs augmented 100×100\times and report task-level Pass@1 on the 149149 test pairs, voting over augmentations. A puzzle is 2525 cell tokens over a 1212-token vocabulary plus the puzzle embedding.

ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2.

The abstraction-and-reasoning benchmarks of Chollet et al. (2024): few-shot tasks in which a grid transformation must be inferred from demonstration pairs and applied to a test grid. Following the HRM/TRM protocol, we train on 960960 (ARC-1) and 1,2801{,}280 (ARC-2) base puzzles, each augmented 1000×1000\times with the transformations of Wang et al. (2025), and report Pass@2 on the 400400 and 120120 evaluation tasks. Grids are padded to 30×3030{\times}30, so a puzzle is a sequence of 900900 cell tokens over a 1212-token vocabulary plus the puzzle embedding.

B.2 Models

SFPRM is implemented in the FPRM code base and shares an identical backbone with 6.836.83M trainable parameters: hidden size 512512, 88 attention heads, MLP expansion 44, rotary position embeddings, and the configuration fields H_cycles/L_cycles/L_layers =3/6/2=3/6/2 of the code base, run as a single weight-tied loop without hierarchy. The number of iterations backpropagated through, is the BPTT window K=6K=6 of Section 3.1.

FPRM. FPRM uses a pre-norm block with the coupled residual-rescaling coefficients (α1,β1,α2,β2)(\alpha_{1},\beta_{1},\alpha_{2},\beta_{2}) of Section 3.1, linear damping, and the relative residual rEr_{\mathrm{E}} with tolerance τE=0.1\tau_{\mathrm{E}}=0.1.

SFPRM. The spherical model replaces the block by the nGPT-style block of Section 3.2: QK-normalized attention and a SwiGLU MLP, each folded into the unit-norm state by an eigen-learning-rate retraction, with all weight vectors renormalized after every optimizer step. Three further choices are specific to SFPRM. (i) The input is injected by the geodesic step of eq. 8 with a learned fraction λ\lambda, initialized at 0.10.1. (ii) The readout is unnormalized: the rows of the output head are not constrained to unit norm, since with a unit-norm state that constraint would cap every logit at ±sz\pm s_{z}, and with it the confidence of the predictions. (iii) The solver is the geodesic one of Algorithm 1, with the chordal residual of eq. 9 and tolerance τc=0.01\tau_{c}=0.01, which corresponds to an angular tolerance of τang=arccos⁡(0.99)≈8.1∘\tau_{\mathrm{ang}}=\arccos(0.99)\approx 8.1^{\circ} per token.

B.3 Training and solver settings

Table 3 lists every hyperparameter. Unless stated otherwise, SFPRM trains with a constant learning rate after the warmup steps and an exponential moving average of the weights with rate 0.9990.999. We optimize SFPRM’s 22-D weight matrices with Muon (Jordan et al., 2024; Pethick et al., 2025) at learning rate 5×10−35\times 10^{-3} and momentum 0.950.95, and its embeddings, normalization scales, and scalar parameters with AdamW at 10−310^{-3}. Weight decay is 0.10.1 for SFPRM, and the per-puzzle embeddings have their own learning rate. SFPRM additionally uses weight dropout and variational dropout of 0.10.1 on the main build (variational dropout only on the 11k×1000\times 1000 Sudoku run). Following the HRM/FPRM code base, one epoch draws one augmented example for every base puzzle; hence 12,00012{,}000 epochs on the 55k×200\times 200 build and 60,00060{,}000 epochs on the 11k×1000\times 1000 build and on Maze-Hard all amount to the same 78,12578{,}125 optimizer steps at a global batch of 768768. For the final Sudoku results, we train for 15,00015{,}000 epochs.

Deep supervision. Training runs one segment of K=6K=6 solver iterations per optimizer step and backpropagates through all KK geodesic steps of the segment; the recurrent state is carried across optimizer steps and detached between segments, and a sample is re-initialized once it halts or once it has been unrolled for max_iter =12=12 iterations. The halting residual, patience counter, step-size schedule, and iterate bookkeeping are evaluated on detached states, so they steer the solver without entering the gradient.

Solver. Both geodesic steps of SFPRM use the guarded interpolation gSlerp\gSlerp of eq. 12. Per sample, the solver keeps the current step size η\eta, the patience counter, the residual, and the residual state. As in FPRM, η\eta starts at 11 and is multiplied by the decay factor γ\gamma whenever the residual has not improved for P=5P=5 consecutive iterations. The loop halts when the residual drops below tolerance, when η\eta falls below the floor ηmin\eta_{\min}, or when the iteration budget is exhausted.

B.4 Evaluation protocol

All tasks are scored by exact accuracy (Pass@1 for Maze-Hard and Sudoku-Extreme and Pass@2 for ARC-1 and ARC-2): a puzzle counts only if every cell is correct, i.e. the whole board or the whole path. We report the final exact test accuracy, except that the SFPRM run on the 11k×1000\times 1000 Sudoku build is reported at both its best and its final evaluation because it collapses between them (Table 4). The published rows of Table 2 are taken from the respective papers.

Appendix C Additional Results, Ablations, and Analysis

This section provides the results that complement Section 4: the Sudoku-Extreme training dataset ablation (Appendix C.1), the Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Hard counterparts of the convergence analyses of Section 4.2 (Appendix C.2), the learned scalars over training (Appendix C.3), additional results on the geometry of the computation (Appendix C.4), and the study of alternative fixed-point solvers at inference (Appendix C.5).

C.1 Training-build ablation

Table 4 compares SFPRM with an FPRM control trained under the same budget on the two Sudoku-Extreme builds described in Appendix B.1. The 55k×200\times 200 does not seem to provide benefits for FPRM, however for SFPRM it removes the collapse happening when training with the 11k×1000\times 1000 build between its best and its final checkpoint.

C.2 Convergence and halting

For Sections 4.2 and 4.3 each trained model is rolled with halting disabled and without segment resets, in fp32, for a fixed budget of Nmax=400N_{\max}=400 iterations on n=512n=512 uniformly sampled test sequences from Sudoku-Extreme and Nmax=1000N_{\max}=1000 on the full Maze-Hard test data. At every iterate 𝐳i\mathbf{z}_{i} the model’s readout head decodes the board, and we record exact and per-token accuracy together with the residual each solver tests: the worst-token chordal residual rc,i=maxt⁡(1−⟨zi,t,z~i,t⟩)r_{\mathrm{c},i}=\max_{t}\bigl(1-\langle z_{i,t},\,\widetilde{z}_{i,t}\rangle\bigr) with τc=0.01\tau_{c}=0.01 for SFPRM, and the worst-token relative residual rE,i=maxt⁡∥zi,t−z~i,t∥∞/∥z~i,t∥∞r_{\mathrm{E},i}=\max_{t}\lVert z_{i,t}-\widetilde{z}_{i,t}\rVert_{\infty}/\lVert\widetilde{z}_{i,t}\rVert_{\infty} with τE=0.1\tau_{\mathrm{E}}=0.1 for FPRM, where 𝐳~i=Fθ​(𝐳i,𝐱)\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}=F_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{i};\mathbf{x}) is each model’s proposal. A sequence counts as halted at the first iteration from which its residual stays below its own threshold. Halt iterations are reported per sequence (mean over the sequences that halt), whereas the deployed evaluator halts a whole batch on its worst sequence, so the per-sequence counts are idealized costs. Every FPRM rollout is generated using the released checkpoints from Movahedi et al. (2026).

Halting. Figure 10 shows the two Sudoku runs of Table 3 (one that reached 92.8%92.8\% and one 96.6%96.6\% exact accuracy) against FPRM. With the learned λ=0.47\lambda=0.47 (left), the median residual of SFPRM drops below τc\tau_{c} within a few dozen iterations, whereas FPRM’s decays roughly geometrically over the whole window. 452452 of the 512512 sequences halt for SFPRM, at a mean of 3333 iterations, against 422422 at a mean of 8989 for FPRM. Exact accuracy is still rising after the mean halt for both models, so on this task the threshold fires before the population has finished improving. With λ\lambda fixed at 0.10.1 (right) the residual of SFPRM decays far more slowly and hovers near τc\tau_{c}, so only 166166 sequences halt within 400400 iterations, at a mean of 254254, although the decoded accuracy is higher. In both runs the puzzles a solver halts on are solved in 99.799.7–100%100\% of cases, so on Sudoku a halt certifies the answer, whereas a missing halt does not certify a failure.

Fixed-point uniqueness. Figure 11 repeats the global-convergence test of Figure 4 on the Maze model (learned λ=0.575\lambda=0.575), running the raw map without damping for 10001000 steps. The contractive regime of Theorem 2 exists here too, but it is narrower: all eight initializations reach the same fixed point only for λ\lambda between about 0.60.6 and 0.80.8. The trained λ\lambda sits at the lower edge of this band, where some mazes have a single end point and others do not, and below λ≈0.5\lambda\approx 0.5 no maze does. For λ≥0.9\lambda\geq 0.9 the end states spread again, while the token accuracy of the fixed point falls to 0.70.7–0.80.8 as the input pulls the state onto itself. On the maze of panel (b) the raw map does not reach the tolerance at the trained λ\lambda within 10001000 steps, although it decodes the maze exactly throughout; it is the damped solver that halts this model. At λ=0.7\lambda=0.7 the raw map converges inside the exact-match region, and at λ=0.9\lambda=0.9 the eight paths run straight to one point that no longer solves the maze.

C.3 Eigen LR and other learnable parameters during training

Figure 12 tracks the learned scalars of SFPRM during training on Maze and Sudoku. Both models raise the injection fraction from 0.10.1 to λ=0.575\lambda=0.575 on Maze and λ=0.470\lambda=0.470 on Sudoku, with most of the increase in the first 30k of 78k training steps. This moves them toward the strong-injection regime of Theorem 2. On Sudoku, all eight initializations already reach the same fixed point on 72% of puzzles at the learned λ\lambda (Figure 4). The logit scale szs_{z} grows almost linearly from 16 to 76, at nearly the same rate on both tasks, and is still rising when training ends. The eigen learning rates keep means near their initial 0.50.5, similarly as noted by Loshchilov et al. (2025). However, individual dimensions spread widely, from negative values, which move the state away from the sub-layer output, to values up to 2.62.6.

C.4 The geometry of the computation

Qualitative results (Figures 7, 21, 22, 23 and 24). We unroll several test puzzles from each task open loop, for 4040 iterations on Maze and Sudoku (rendered at t=0,2,11,39t=0,2,11,39) and 200200 on Mini-ARC (rendered at t=0,3,13,52,199t=0,3,13,52,199). The decoded board is the per-cell argmax of the readout. The anchor map shows, per cell, the angle ∠⁡(zi,t,x^i)\angle(z_{i,t},\hat{x}_{i}) between the iterate and its unit-normalized input embedding x^i\hat{x}_{i} (token plus position), on a colour scale normalized to the minimum and maximum angle over that puzzle’s whole rollout, so that a colour means the same angle in every frame of a strip. The same quantity is computed for FPRM from its unnormalized state. SFPRM’s anchor angles separate the roles of the cells far more cleanly than FPRM’s: on Sudoku, clue cells end 35∘35^{\circ} closer to their anchors than blank cells, against 6∘6^{\circ} for FPRM, and on Mini-ARC the cells a task must rewrite end furthest from their anchors (AUC 0.810.81 for changed vs. unchanged cells, averaged over tasks), whereas FPRM’s ordering flips from task to task (AUC 0.510.51).

Anchor angles by cell class (Figures 15, 6 and 16). For four Sudoku and Maze test puzzles, we track the anchor angle of every cell throughout the unrolling, grouped by cell class (clues and blanks on Sudoku; walls, free cells that stay empty, free cells that become path, start, and goal on Maze). In the figures, the heavy lines are class means, whilst the thin lines show the individual cells’ anchor angles. The histograms on the right-hand side of each figure show the distribution at the end of the unrolling (i=399i=399 on Sudoku, 999999 on Maze). For FPRM the angle is that of the normalized state.

Trajectories on the sphere (Figure 14). We draw each token’s path in the frame spanned by the inference unrolling trajectory’s two leading singular directions and its input anchor 𝐱\mathbf{x}. This way the anchor is exact rather than a near-zero projection. We only show the cell trajectories that capture the most trajectory variance. Over 98%98\% of each trajectory’s variance lies in that frame, so every token effectively moves on one great circle, as the geodesic steps of Algorithm 1 prescribe, and the anchor sits nearly orthogonal to that circle (|⟨xt,v1,2⟩|≈0.05|\langle x_{t},\,v_{1,2}\rangle|\approx 0.05). The input injection pulls from far off the plane in which the computation happens, explaining how a small λ\lambda can anchor the hidden state without dictating it.

Solved versus unsolved (Figure 9). For 128128 Sudoku test puzzles we compare the distribution of the final anchor angle (SFPRM) or final norm (FPRM) of clue and blank cells between solved and unsolved puzzles. The same comparison on 512512 test mazes (Figure 13) shows no separation for either model.

C.5 Fixed-point solvers at inference

Both SFPRM and FPRM are trained with a damped fixed-point iteration, but at inference any method that finds a fixed point of Fθ​(⋅,𝐱)F_{\theta}(\cdot\,;\mathbf{x}) can take its place. We run four solvers (including the default one) on the trained models, without retraining and without changing the architecture (see Section 4.2).

C.5.1 Solvers

All four solvers seek a fixed point of the same trained map. The model weights are unchanged, and only the default solver (adaptive) was used during training. At test time the input embedding 𝐱\mathbf{x} is computed once and every solver runs the loop

𝐳~i=Fθ​(𝐳i,𝐱),stop if ​ri<τ,𝐳i+1=update⁡(𝐳i,𝐳~i,history),\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}=F_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{i};\mathbf{x}),\qquad\text{stop if }r_{i}<\tau,\qquad\mathbf{z}_{i+1}=\mathrm{update}\bigl(\mathbf{z}_{i},\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i},\text{history}\bigr),

starting from a random 𝐳0\mathbf{z}_{0}. Across solvers, only the update function differs. Each step evaluates FθF_{\theta} once, and the same evaluation gives the halting residual, so the number of steps is the compute spent. SFPRM halts on the chordal residual ri=rc,ir_{i}=r_{\mathrm{c},i} of eq. 9 with τc=0.01\tau_{c}=0.01, and FPRM on the per-token relative residual ri=rE,i=maxt⁡∥zi,t−z~i,t∥∞/∥z~i,t∥∞r_{i}=r_{\mathrm{E},i}=\max_{t}\lVert z_{i,t}-\widetilde{z}_{i,t}\rVert_{\infty}/\lVert\widetilde{z}_{i,t}\rVert_{\infty} (eq. 4) with τE=0.1\tau_{\mathrm{E}}=0.1. We write 𝐠i:=𝐳~i−𝐳i\mathbf{g}_{i}:=\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}-\mathbf{z}_{i} for the residual vector. Two operators adapt the updates to each model’s state space: the interpolation ℐη​(𝐚,𝐛)\mathcal{I}_{\eta}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}) moves 𝐚\mathbf{a} a fraction η\eta of the way to 𝐛\mathbf{b}, along the great circle token by token for SFPRM, ℐη=Slerpη\mathcal{I}_{\eta}=\Slerp_{\eta} as in eq. 7, and along the straight line for FPRM, ℐη​(𝐚,𝐛)=(1−η)​𝐚+η​𝐛\mathcal{I}_{\eta}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})=(1-\eta)\mathbf{a}+\eta\mathbf{b} as in eq. 3; the projection Π\Pi applies Norm\Norm to every token for SFPRM and is the identity for FPRM.

Adaptive (default). 𝐳i+1=ℐηi​(𝐳i,𝐳~i)\mathbf{z}_{i+1}=\mathcal{I}_{\eta_{i}}(\mathbf{z}_{i},\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}) with η0=1\eta_{0}=1. The step size is multiplied by γ=0.99\gamma=0.99 whenever the residual has not improved for P=5P=5 consecutive steps while it is still above τ\tau. Both models are trained and evaluated with this solver.

Fixed step. The same update with ηi=1\eta_{i}=1 throughout, that is, plain fixed-point iteration 𝐳i+1=𝐳~i\mathbf{z}_{i+1}=\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}.

Anderson acceleration (Anderson, 1965; Walker and Ni, 2011) replaces the latest state by the combination of the last m+1m+1 states whose residuals cancel best. With the columns of Δ​𝐆i\Delta\mathbf{G}_{i} and Δ​𝐙~i\Delta\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{i} the mm differences of consecutive stored residuals and images,

𝝎i=arg⁡min𝝎∈ℝm⁡∥𝐠i−Δ​𝐆i​𝝎∥22+δ​∥𝝎∥22,𝐳i+1=Π⁡(𝐳~i−Δ​𝐙~i​𝝎i),\boldsymbol{\omega}_{i}=\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}}\,\lVert\mathbf{g}_{i}-\Delta\mathbf{G}_{i}\boldsymbol{\omega}\rVert_{2}^{2}+\delta\lVert\boldsymbol{\omega}\rVert_{2}^{2},\qquad\mathbf{z}_{i+1}=\Pi\bigl(\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}-\Delta\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{i}\boldsymbol{\omega}_{i}\bigr),

with a small ridge δ>0\delta>0. The least-squares problem learns, from the recent iterates alone, how the residual responds to a change of state, and the combination removes the components that the plain step overshoots, so an oscillation across the fixed point, for example, cancels between consecutive states. We use memory m=3m=3.

Broyden’s method (Broyden, 1965), the solver commonly used for deep equilibrium models (Bai et al., 2019), takes quasi-Newton steps on 𝐠⁡(𝐳)=Fθ​(𝐳,𝐱)−𝐳\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{z})=F_{\theta}(\mathbf{z};\mathbf{x})-\mathbf{z} with an estimate 𝐁i\mathbf{B}_{i} of the inverse Jacobian of 𝐠\mathbf{g}:

𝐳i+1=Π⁡(𝐳i−𝐁i​𝐠i),𝐁i=𝐁i−1+(𝐬i−𝐁i−1​𝐲i)​𝐬i⊤​𝐁i−1𝐬i⊤​𝐁i−1​𝐲i,\mathbf{z}_{i+1}=\Pi\bigl(\mathbf{z}_{i}-\mathbf{B}_{i}\mathbf{g}_{i}\bigr),\qquad\mathbf{B}_{i}=\mathbf{B}_{i-1}+\frac{(\mathbf{s}_{i}-\mathbf{B}_{i-1}\mathbf{y}_{i})\,\mathbf{s}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{B}_{i-1}}{\mathbf{s}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{B}_{i-1}\mathbf{y}_{i}},

where 𝐬i=𝐳i−𝐳i−1\mathbf{s}_{i}=\mathbf{z}_{i}-\mathbf{z}_{i-1} and 𝐲i=𝐠i−𝐠i−1\mathbf{y}_{i}=\mathbf{g}_{i}-\mathbf{g}_{i-1}. Starting from 𝐁0=−𝐈\mathbf{B}_{0}=-\mathbf{I}, the estimate is stored as the last m=5m=5 rank-one corrections.

Neither Anderson’s nor Broyden’s method computes a Jacobian or any gradient. Both are quasi-Newton methods that infer curvature from secants, the observed changes of state and residual between steps, so each step still costs one evaluation of FθF_{\theta}. With an empty memory both take exactly the fixed step. Both act on the whole state of an example at once, all tokens flattened into one vector, with one history per example in a batch. Their extrapolated points leave the sphere and are projected back by Π\Pi. The extra work per step is a few vector operations on the state and an m×mm\times m linear solve, and the extra memory is mm stored copies of the state, both small next to an evaluation of FθF_{\theta}. As safeguards, a non-finite extrapolation falls back to the fixed step, and Broyden skips an update whose denominator is near zero. Both methods use the step size η=1\eta=1 (no damping).

C.5.2 Results

We run every solver on all 1000 Maze test examples and on 1000 Sudoku test puzzles spaced evenly over the 422,786-puzzle test set, in fp32, with SFPRM at its trained injection fraction (λ=0.575\lambda=0.575 on Maze, λ=0.1\lambda=0.1 on Sudoku) and FPRM from its released checkpoints. Each example starts from its own random state (uniform on the sphere for SFPRM, the truncated normal of the FPRM solver for FPRM), shared by the four solvers, and is iterated for 1000 steps. We then apply the halting rule to each example separately: the answer is the first iterate whose residual is below τ\tau, and an example that never halts is answered by its iterate at step 1000. Table 5 reports the results, and Figures 5 and 17 show accuracy and residual over the iterations in the four settings.

The undamped step does not halt reliably. The fixed step never reaches τ\tau on 37%, 100%, 49% and 56% of the examples in the four settings. For SFPRM on Maze its answers are identical to the default solver’s, but on Sudoku it is less accurate for both models. For SFPRM on Sudoku a quarter of the puzzles do not halt within 1000 steps.

Anderson acceleration matches the default solver at a fraction of the cost. Its accuracy at the halt is within one point of the default solver’s in all four settings. Anderson halts earlier in every setting, with a striking 37 against 435 for SFPRM on Sudoku. Averaged over all examples, this is 9×\times fewer evaluations of FθF_{\theta}. For FPRM on Sudoku the saving disappears (190 against 200 evaluations): 10.8% of the puzzles never reach τ\tau under Anderson, and all of them are answered incorrectly.

Broyden’s method reaches the tolerance threshold quickly but does not stay there. On Maze it halts as early as Anderson (14 and 16 median steps), and its halted answers are as accurate as the default solver’s. By continuing to iterate beyond the tolerance, however, it leaves the fixed point and its accuracy degrades, making it usable only with halting.

On Sudoku, halting certifies the answer. For SFPRM on Sudoku, 99.7–100% of the puzzles a solver halts on are solved exactly, so the accuracy differences come entirely from the puzzles it fails to halt on. The same holds less strictly for FPRM (96.2% of the default solver’s halted puzzles are solved, 99.6% of Anderson’s). On Maze, halting does not certify the answer: incorrect mazes converge too, and for the solvers that halt on almost every example the accuracy among halted examples is about the same as the overall accuracy.

Trajectories in the principal plane. Figure 18 shows the four solvers at the trained λ\lambda in the plane construction of Figure 4b, on a single test example from each task, from eight initializations. The reference 𝐳⋆\mathbf{z}^{\star} is Anderson’s end point, a fixed point to fp32 precision that decodes both examples exactly. On Maze, Anderson halts at iteration 1313 from all eight initializations, the default solver crosses the tolerance at a median of 140140 iterations but ends 0.060.06 rad away, and fixed η=1\eta=1 never crosses it. On the Sudoku puzzle only Anderson halts (median 4040), while the default and fixed solvers end 0.160.16 and 0.330.33 rad from 𝐳⋆\mathbf{z}^{\star} and still decode the puzzle exactly. Broyden reaches the tolerance as early as Anderson and then leaves from most starts.

Trajectories in polar coordinates. Figures 19 and 20 follow one token per cell class under each solver in the polar view of Figure 5b, for the maze of that panel and for a Sudoku puzzle. The radius is the geodesic angle to a common reference, Anderson’s end point after 20002000 iterations, a fixed point to fp32 precision that decodes both examples exactly. Inward is convergence toward 𝐳⋆\mathbf{z}^{\star}, a held radius is orbiting, and outward is leaving. Anderson ends within 10−410^{-4} degrees of the reference. The default solver ends 0.0050.005–0.14∘0.14^{\circ} away on the mazes and up to 2.1∘2.1^{\circ} on the Sudoku puzzles, after orbiting for hundreds of iterations; fixed η=1\eta=1 stays up to 0.64∘0.64^{\circ} and 44–17∘17^{\circ} away and never halts; and Broyden reaches the tolerance first and then leaves to 6060–103∘103^{\circ}.

C.6 ARC-AGI-2 Results

We compute the Pass@2 on the 120120 evaluation tasks of ARC-AGI-2. All models remain far from solving the benchmark. The best recurrent reasoner, TRM, reaches 7.8%7.8\%, and SFPRM reaches 3.8%3.8\%. The gaps nonetheless amount to only a few tasks, so we do not draw strong conclusions from them. At 77M parameters, SFPRM still outperforms reasoning LLMs, including o3-mini-high (3.0%3.0\%), DeepSeek-R1 (1.3%1.3\%) and Claude 3.7 (0.7%0.7\%).

C.7 Algorithmic Ablations

Table 6 retrains the Mini-ARC model with one component of SFPRM changed at a time. QK normalization is essential, and removing the step damping (η=1\eta=1) or fixing the input-injection fraction costs 11.4 and 9.4 points, respectively. The remaining changes, including ACT halting in place of the chordal residual, cost at most 4.7 points.

Appendix D Limitations

On the theory side, Theorem 1 certifies a step-size window but not that the patience rule finds it, and Theorem 2 covers only strong injection. On the experimental side, every run uses a single seed and neither model was tuned beyond FPRM’s recipe: a broader hyperparameter search, stronger regularization, and optimizers that exploit the spherical geometry further would likely improve both. Two directions remain open. Attention-free MLP-Mixer blocks have been reported to beat Transformer blocks on some of these puzzles (Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025; Sghaier et al., 2026; Suleymanzade et al., 2026); the spherical loop is agnostic to the block and could be combined with them. And we have not applied SFPRM to language modeling, where looped Transformers are gaining ground (Geiping et al., 2025; Prairie et al., 2026) and where halting on a fixed angular tolerance may be most valuable.
